reputation.summary: Linear's datasheets call the LT1468/LT1469 'optimum' for high-accuracy uses such as DAC current-to-voltage conversion and ADC buffers, and show an 'Ultralow Distortion Balanced Audio Line Driver' at 0.00025% THD+N (with an LT1364 supplying output current). On diyAudio, members describe it as as clean as the OPA627 but quieter and more neutral, and a better I/V choice than the OPA627; one poster, citing Samuel Groner's op-amp measurement shootout, concluded the LT1469 'should be the best of the bunch overall'. Views are not unanimous: it has been called 'rather thin, very clean', one user heard 'metallic' treble (possibly a bypassing problem), and some say it lacks output current and 'character' for a final output stage. These are forum opinions, not measurements. The specific 'very low common-mode distortion' reading of Groner's survey was not confirmed.
typical_uses: I/V conversion for current-output DACs (datasheet front-page LTC1597 example; diyAudio I/V threads)
DAC post-filter / active reconstruction filters
ADC input buffer / driver (datasheet LTC1604 example)
balanced line driver (datasheet parallel-composite circuit with LT1364)
op-amp rolling in DAC output stages (community)
caveats: The -2 variants (LT1468-2 / LT1469-2) are stable only at gain ≥ 2 and may oscillate in unity-gain buffer sockets. Check the suffix.
Phase reversal (datasheet): if an input comes within 0.5 V of the positive supply, the output reverses phase.

Layout-sensitive. The datasheet asks for a ground plane, short leads, RF-quality 0.01-0.1 µF bypass capacitors in parallel with 1-10 µF low-ESR capacitors, and guard rings for best DC. Socket adapters and long leads likely raise the oscillation risk (general inference). A diyAudio report of 'metallic' treble was attributed to inadequate bypassing.

Input-capacitance pole: for RF > 2k use CF > RG·CIN/RF. When DC noise gain is one with a large RF, CF should be ≥ CIN, and a DAC can add 'many tens of pF'. The datasheet's LTC1597 I/V uses 15 pF across 12k for optimum nulling.
Capacitive load is limited to 100 pF at unity gain and 300 pF at gain -1. Beyond that, use a series output resistor plus a feedback capacitor (datasheet Fig. 3).

Because of bias-current cancellation, the datasheet says balanced source resistances are NOT recommended: they degrade DC accuracy and raise noise. The noninverting-input IB is untrimmed (±40 nA max).
Modest output current (±22 mA typ; diyAudio posters note ~20 mA as a limit for final output use). The datasheet line driver adds an LT1364 to drive 600 Ω.
Draws about 4.1 mA per amplifier at ±15 V (up to 6.5 mA over temperature), so it runs warmer than low-power audio duals.
Needs a proper split supply: specified at ±5 V and ±15 V, with ±4.5 V the guaranteed minimum.

Simulation: older LTspice IV symbols (mirrored on GitHub) describe LT1468-2 and LT1469-2 as '90MHz, 22V/µs', and the LT1469 and LT1469-2 symbols reference the single-channel LT1468 and LT1468-2 models. ADI fixed the LT1468-2 label on 01/23/21.

families.technology: JFET-input single op-amp. Launch coverage (EE Times Japan 'Only one channel, yet two chips!' and Stereo Sound, both 2017-03-24) describes a two-chip build with separate input-stage and output-stage dies. reputation.summary: Launched in March 2017 as New JRC's MUSES flagship single. Launch press (Stereo Sound: 'Will it reach the summit of op-amps?'; EE Times Japan) focused on the two-die design and the 0.00003% THD. Head-Fi Opamp-thread posters (seen as search summaries, not full threads) credit its midrange and a deliberately 'slow' presentation that gives vocals and instruments physical presence and holography. They call it neutral with a slightly darker tone than the OPA828 or AD797BRZ, and one poster found the OPA828 emotionally flat on vocals by comparison. Posters describe the later MUSES05 as a refinement with more speed, resolution and air, and the MUSES03 as having more body. They also rate the MUSES03 less resolving than the Burson V7 Vivid. The PHILE WEB MUSES05 launch report credits the MUSES05 with deeper staging. Views are not unanimous: a Japanese blogger could not tell the MUSES03D from the MUSES05 in a Quad405 copy amp. No independent bench measurements (ASR, Samuel Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: midrange strength; a deliberately 'slow' sound that gives vocals and instruments physical presence and holography (Head-Fi Opamp thread, via search summary)
power and presence projected by vocalists (diyAudio/Head-Fi, via search summary)
neutral, with a slightly darker tone than the OPA828 or AD797BRZ (Head-Fi, via search summary)
more body, but less air, speed and resolution, than the MUSES05 (Head-Fi Opamp thread)
less resolving than the Burson V7 Vivid (Head-Fi Opamp thread)
less three-dimensional depth than the MUSES05 (PHILE WEB MUSES05 launch listening report)
typical_uses: I/V conversion after DACs (datasheet application list)
preamps, line amps and active filters (datasheet)
headphone amps (datasheet list; 250 mA peak abs-max output, which community posts say is well above the 30–100 mA typical of rivals)
op-amp rolling with two singles on a dual-DIP8 adapter in DACs and headphone amps (hobbyist use)
caveats: Single channel, DIP8 only: a dual socket needs two parts on an adapter, which adds height and lead length.
Iq is 5.8 mA typ and 10 mA max per amplifier, so a two-part adapter can draw 20 mA per socket. Check regulators and heat.
Minimum supply is ±3.5 V and abs max is ±19 V. Differential input abs max is only ±6 V.
The output is asymmetric under heavy load: about -10 V into 50 Ω and about -6 V at 250 mA on the negative side, against about +12.6/+12.8 V on the positive side (datasheet graphs).
Peak output abs max is 250 mA. The datasheet recommends a series protection resistor (e.g. ≥90 Ω at 18 V) where a short is possible.
Slew rate is asymmetric on the datasheet graph: about 37 V/µs rising versus about 102 V/µs falling.
Vos is 1.0 mV typ with no max. Ib is several hundred pA at 85 °C and reaches the nA range above about 90 °C.
Listening impressions are subjective and mixed: one blogger heard no clear difference from the MUSES05.
Discontinued by Oct 2023. Stock is scarce, much of the remaining supply trades on auction and marketplace sites, and counterfeits of MUSES parts are reported.

families.counterfeit_notes: Vendor, datasheet Ver.4.2 p.10: counterfeit MUSES parts circulate worldwide and are often visually indistinguishable from genuine ones. NJR says to buy only through its sales offices or authorized distributors. Genuine reference points from the datasheet: marking '03' (ordering table; alldatasheet marking page); package DIP8(MUSES), body 8.8 × 6.4 mm, OFC lead frame; Sn-2Bi plating; 470 mg; shipped in carbon sticks of 10. Since the 2023 EOL, much of the remaining supply is on auction and marketplace sites (Yahoo! Auctions and aucfan listings seen), where fakes are the main risk. Hobbyist warning (maimai-audio blog 'オペアンプの偽物に注意しよう！', medium-low confidence): it names MUSES01/02/03 among models needing caution, especially units priced far below list or appearing in quantity after production ended. The nw-electric blog (2019) recommends slew-rate measurement as the most effective generic fake test; for MUSES03 the reference values are SR+ about 37 and SR- about 102 V/µs, Iq about 5.8 mA. The 'MUSES03D' name on Akizuki stock is a retailer catalog name, not a sign of a fake. No decap or teardown evidence was found.
alternatives: MUSES05 (Nisshinbo): the successor flagship JFET single, two-chip and fully balanced; general sale from Feb 2022. Its production was reported halted over a process-material shortage (nw-electric 2024-06), and a search summary also calls it discontinued, so check its current status.
OPA828 (TI): a low-noise JFET single that community reports compare with MUSES03
OPA1641 / OPA1656 (TI): current SoundPlus FET-input parts
MUSES01 (NJR/Nisshinbo): JFET-input dual in the MUSES line
OPA627 (TI/Burr-Brown): the legacy JFET-single benchmark, heavily counterfeited
MUSES8920A (Nisshinbo): the budget JFET dual

reputation.summary: Often called the 'budget MUSES02' and treated as the value way into the MUSES sound. Japanese blog reviews (tanupon2000, 音フェチの世界, guiblo/zigsow, new_western_elec) describe it as close to MUSES02 with slightly thinner lines. They report full, deep bass and a crisp, forward presentation, with the extreme treble slightly softened. One LT1364 comparison calls it warmer, with more bass. Head-Fi posters (the Opamp thread and the Burson V6 Classic round-up) called it 'least opamp-sounding', tube-like and wide-staged; one heard no difference from MUSES02 in an LPF position. Rankings put it above NJM4580/NJM8801 and below newer or JFET parts: new_western_elec (2025) ranked OPA2604 < MUSES8820 < MUSES8920 < NL8802 < NL8902. OEM uses include the TEAC AP-507 (MUSES8820E), the Ibanez BT Mini and the VentureCraft VALOQ.
sonic_descriptors: close to MUSES02 but thinner lines
typical_uses: Drop-in upgrade for NJM4580/NE5532 sockets in DACs, CD players and preamps
Op-amp rolling in socketed DIP-8 headphone amps and DACs
DIY preamp, line and LPF stages
OEM: TEAC AP-507 (MUSES8820E), Ibanez BT Mini bass pedal, VentureCraft VALOQ
caveats: All praise is subjective listening impressions. No ASR or Samuel Groner bench data was found, and the Head-Fi round-up's measurement values were not captured.
The 'least opamp-sounding / almost as good as OPA627' quotes may come from the Opamp thread rather than the Burson V6 round-up, which has no OPA627.
Bipolar input: bias current is 100 nA typ / 500 nA max, far above FET parts such as MUSES8920. Watch high source impedances and DC-coupled pots.
Output drive, stability and full electrical tables were not read. Check the datasheet before driving headphones directly.
Counterfeits are documented for MUSES01, MUSES02 and MUSES8920D; no MUSES8820-specific case was found.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented MUSES8820-specific fake was found. Fakes are documented for sibling MUSES parts: MUSES01 and MUSES02 fakes posted by @fakecomponents on X, including a MUSES02 fake passed off as an Akizuki purchase with thin, wrong top-marking digits, and a MUSES8920D fake reported by new_western_elec (2023-11). MUSES parts in general are reported as frequent counterfeit targets on AliExpress. Practical checks: buy from DigiKey, Mouser or Japanese retailers (Akizuki, Kyohritsu eleshop, Marutsu); treat prices far below the roughly ¥1,100 retail price for MUSES8820D with suspicion; compare the top-marking font, logo and lot code with a known-genuine part; and measure input bias current (100 nA typ / 500 nA max) or supply current against the datasheet. Logo or marking differences between New JRC-era and Nisshinbo-era lots are unverified.

families.tagline: A cheap, quiet JRC bipolar dual. NwAvGuy used it for the O2's gain stage, and it is common in E-MU audio interfaces and in Japanese CD and AV gear.

reputation.summary: NwAvGuy measured the NJM2068 for the Objective2 (O2) and chose it for the gain stage. By his account it was quieter than the NE5532, LM4562 and OPA2134 at lower supply current, and it cost well under a dollar. That made it a favourite with the measurement-minded DIY community. The DIY SmartStand amp also copies the O2's NJM2068 gain stage with an NJM4556A output. In China, Soomal reviews found it in E-MU interfaces (0202/0204/0404/1212m), the Musiland X-Sword II and ooAoo sound cards, and many mid-range CD players. Soomal describes it as very low noise and high resolution, with a neutral, plain sound. Japanese op-amp swappers treat it as the classic quiet JRC dual, calling it relaxed with ample bass. Pro and MI gear uses it too: the Roland VG-99 input stage and GK-3 pickup (per h-milz), Yamaha and Pioneer AV and car units, and cheap MM phono preamps such as FX-Audio. The sound descriptors are community impressions, not measurements.
sonic_descriptors: very low noise (噪声很小; Soomal)
typical_uses: O2 (Objective2) headphone amp gain stage
E-MU 0202/0204/0404/1212m audio interfaces
Chinese PC sound cards (Musiland X-Sword II, ooAoo SQ710 II/SQ717a)
mid-range Japanese CD players and AV receivers (e.g. Yamaha YSP-600 uses NJM2068MD-TE2)
car audio (Pioneer KEX-M8406ZT, NJM2068MD)
MM phono / RIAA preamps (FX-Audio BOX-01/BOX-02)
guitar-synth/pro-audio input stages (Roland VG-99, GK-3 per h-milz)
active monitor speakers (ICON PX-T6A per Soomal)
caveats: Vendor notice: capacitive loads can cause oscillation. Add about 50 Ohm in series with the output (Ver.2011-03-18 p.2).
Minimum supply is +/-4 V (8 V total), so it is unsuitable for 5 V single-supply or USB-powered designs.
The '27 MHz' headline figure is GB at 10 kHz. The unity-gain frequency is only 5.5 MHz, so it is not comparable with other vendors' GBW numbers.
No noise-current or nV/rtHz spec, and input bias current is relatively high (150 nA typ, 1 uA max). Keep source and feedback impedances low.
Output current is not specified, and specs are given for loads of 2 kOhm and above. It is not a headphone driver: the O2 pairs it with NJM4556A outputs.

jh4vaj's pop-noise comparison found the standard NJM2068D had less turn-on pop than the noise-selected NJM2068DD. Both were among the low-pop group; NJM4558DD had the least. This is a single blog measurement.
A note.com blog (gokurakugadget) reports NJM2068D oscillating abnormally in an audio preamp. It is a single user report; see the vendor capacitive-load notice.

families.counterfeit_notes: No NJM2068-specific counterfeit or remarking reports were found in a limited web search. Generic Amazon and eBay listings sell 'NJM2068M SOP8 JRC2068' in lots of 5-10 from unnamed sellers. As with other popular 'JRC' audio duals, such marketplace parts carry a general risk of being remarked. Buy from authorized distributors (Mouser, DigiKey, Akizuki). A 'DD'/'MD' marking only means noise-selected, not a different die, so a big price premium for 'DD' from unknown sellers deserves suspicion. Check the logo style, lot codes and package: genuine DMP8 has a 5.3 mm-wide body, not a 3.9 mm JEDEC SOIC, even though listings call it 'SOP8'.

reputation.summary: A mid-tier Japanese audio dual, marketed by JRC as an improved NJM5532 and perceived that way. JP DIY reviews of NJM2114DD are mostly positive: a Zigsow review is titled 'same price class as NE5532 but better sound', and reviewers describe clear, firm bass and more clarity than NJM2068. Opinion is not unanimous: one JP comparison ranks NJM2114 (with NJM4580) C-rank, below NE5532, LM4562 and OPA2134 (B-rank). Internationally it is best known as the stock JRC2114(D) in the Creative X-Fi Titanium HD, Zx, ZxR, X7 and AE-9, the ASUS Xonar Essence STX, the Gigabyte Z170X-Gaming G1 and the TempoTec DAII Plus. Soomal considers it a neutral buffer/I-V part. No independent measurements were found.
sonic_descriptors: 'Same price class as NE5532 but better sound' (Zigsow NJM2114DD review title)
clear, firm bass with relatively subdued highs (JP NJM2114DD reviews, via search summary)
not bass-heavy like NJM5532; drier than OPA2134; slightly more coloured than LME49860 (JP reviews, via search summary)
'higher-performance 2068: wins on information and clarity' (JP comparison, via search summary)
'JRC2114对声音影响较小': has relatively little effect on the sound (Soomal AE-9 review, 2020)
typical_uses: Creative Sound Blaster X-Fi Titanium HD (2010): socketed JRC2114D, presumed filter and I/V, with LME49710 singles (Soomal)
Creative Sound Blaster ZxR (2013): socketed NJM2114D + LME49710 on front channels, SMD JRC2114 on others. Creative spec: 'Headphone Op-Amps (Swappable) NJM2114D', TPA6120A2 driver.
Creative Sound Blaster Zx (2013) and Sound Blaster X7 (2015, JRC2114D + LME49710) (Soomal)
Creative Sound Blaster AE-9 (2020): socketed JRC2114 buffer with NE5534 singles; SMD JRC2114 + L49720 on sub-channels (Soomal)
ASUS Xonar Essence STX (2009): socketed 2114D used as the I/V converter (Soomal)
E-MU 0202 USB (Soomal teardown, 2010); Gigabyte Z170X-Gaming G1 onboard audio (2015); TempoTec Fantasia DAII Plus DAC, two 2114D as I/V (2017)
I/V stage in some Philips / Marantz CD players (head-fi opamp thread p.113; models unverified, low confidence)
Drop-in NJM5532 / NJM2068 / NJM4580 swap in Japanese headphone amps, USB-DAC filters and cassette decks
caveats: Soomal's AE-9 review (2020-04-15) says op-amps on Creative's EARLIER cards were already good, so swapping brought almost no improvement. It calls the AE-9's stock NE5534 singles puzzling, and advises that users wanting a different sound should upgrade the two singles (LME49710 for continuity) rather than the JRC2114.
Mixed JP rankings: one comparison surfaced by search ranks it C-rank, below NE5532. The page was not pinned; the candidate is nabe.adiary.jp/opamp-compare.

Availability: a 2023 JP blog reports that Nisshinbo made it a maintenance (pre-EOL, not for new designs) product. Marutsu has ended sales of NJM2114D and Mouser shows NJM2114L as obsolete. Expect shrinking authorised stock and more grey-market parts.

No objective measurements (ASR, Groner, jh4vaj) were found. Treat it as a 5532-class bipolar NPN-input part: input bias current and source impedance matter, and with 13 MHz GBW and 15 V/µs it needs sensible decoupling and layout.

families.name: NJM4556 / NJM4556A (dual high-output-current bipolar, 70 mA)
families.tagline: JRC's 70 mA dual that drives 150 ohm loads directly. It is the paralleled output stage of NwAvGuy's O2 and a staple of Japanese DIY headphone amps.
families.technology: Bipolar dual op-amp with a high-current output stage (+/-70 mA into 150 ohm at +/-10.5 V). The input differential pair is PNP in the datasheet equivalent circuit, in NJR's own PSpice macromodels (Version 1 and 2) and in the 2007 Bee Technologies model. Supply is +/-2 V to +/-18 V. The datasheet says it combines many NJM4558 features with 150 ohm drive capability. The Japanese search summary describes it as a 4558 with a reinforced output stage. On the typical curve at +/-15 V, the output sources about 100 mA and sinks about 200 mA before swing collapses.

reputation.summary: It is valued for current drive rather than for a distinctive sound. NwAvGuy used NJM4556A in the current-gain (output) stage of the Objective2 (O2), with both halves paralleled per channel. An earlier search summary of his 'O2 Details' page paraphrased him as saying no other dual DIP8 op-amp delivered as much current at as low distortion ('killed everything else'); this pass did not re-confirm that wording. The O2 made it a default DIY headphone driver, reused in O2/ODA derivatives, Eurorack headphone modules and other projects. Japanese DIY sources call it a standard (定番) headphone-amp chip, and say it sounds surprisingly good for about 30 yen. One Japanese listening comparison (audio-simulation.net, 2019) found it more energetic but rougher in texture than the NJM4580. It also appears in commercial gear: one 2018 owner's Behringer UCA202 had a 4556A, and the Roland AC-90 uses NJM4556AM in its phones amp.
sonic_descriptors: energetic / lively (vs NJM4580; single Japanese listening test)
surprisingly good for the price (Japanese DIY summary)
clean, low-distortion current drive (NwAvGuy O2 testing)
typical_uses: O2 / ODA headphone amp output stage (paralleled sections)
DIY and kit headphone amps in Japan (e.g. aitendo kits)
Eurorack headphone and line-out modules (NJM4556AV)
USB audio interface headphone outputs (one 2018 teardown of a Behringer UCA202)
instrument-amp phones outputs (Roland AC-90, NJM4556AM)
line drivers into 150-600 ohm loads
caveats: The DIP8 (NJM4556AD) and SIP8 (AL) versions are NRND per the March 2025 Nisshinbo datasheet. A maintenance-product (保守品) designation was reported in April 2023. The SMD AM and AV versions continue.
The SMD packages are JRC DMP8 (wider body than a 3.9 mm JEDEC SOIC-8) and SSOP8, so footprints differ.
Package dissipation limits are low (DMP8 300 mW, SSOP8 250 mW), and quiescent current is 9 mA typ per package. Derate for high rails and low-impedance headphones.
Speed is modest (3 V/us, 8 MHz). The typical THD at 20 kHz rises steeply with output level (about 0.2% at 10 Vrms into 200 ohm).
High offset (6 mV max) and bias current (500 nA max) matter in DC-coupled designs like the O2.
Its reputation rests on drive capability rather than a distinctive sound. The sonic descriptors come from single listening reports.

A '4556' on vintage boards may be NEC's uPC4556. That part is decompensated (stable only at gain >= 20 dB), so it is not a substitute for an NJM4556 in a unity-gain buffer. It may also be a Yamaha house-marked part.

silicon_changes.audio_impact: A uPC4556 placed in an NJM4556 socket at unity or low gain (e.g. the O2 output buffer) risks oscillation, and its heavy-load drive is unknown. An NJM4556A replacing a uPC4556 in a high-gain vintage stage would lose bandwidth and slew.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: high: a decompensated part is not a drop-in for unity-gain buffer or driver roles, and the pinout is the standard dual but the stability requirements differ

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit or remarking reports for NJM4556/NJM4556A were found; search coverage was limited. eBay listings of NJM4556AD advertised as '"Original" JRC' show that DIP stock now circulates on the grey market after the NRND notice; the 2023 保守品 report and the March 2025 datasheet both mark AD/AL as NRND. Remarked 4558/4559-class duals would not deliver 70 mA (unverified risk). Salvaged vintage '4556' parts may be NEC uPC4556, a decompensated part that is unstable at unity gain and not an equivalent, or Yamaha house-marked YM4556 parts. A practical check: at +/-15 V a genuine NJM4556A should hold about +/-11 V into 150 ohm (datasheet min +/-10.5 V), draw about 9 mA per package, and be stable as a unity-gain follower. Buy from authorized Nisshinbo distributors.

families.name: OP27 / OP37 (PMI/ADI low-noise precision bipolar; OP37 = decompensated, gain ≥5)
families.tagline: PMI's c.1980 3 nV/√Hz zener-trimmed precision bipolar op-amp, long used in phono, tape-head and mic preamps; ADI's datasheet still carries those audio circuits.
families.technology: Monolithic bipolar, single channel (PMI/ADI design described here). NPN input stage at high quiescent current for low e_n, input bias-current cancellation, back-to-back input clamp diodes without series resistors, and zener-zap offset trim at wafer test. OP27 is unity-gain stable (8 MHz, 2.8 V/µs). OP37 is the same design decompensated for closed-loop gain ≥5 (63 MHz, 17 V/µs). Linear Technology and Texas Instruments sold their own OP27/OP37 under the same part numbers; their die designs are not documented.
manufacturers: Analog Devices (acquired PMI c.1990; current source; also keeps a separate 'OP27-LTC' product page from the Linear Technology line)
Linear Technology (OP-27/OP-37/OP-227/OP-237 second source; datasheets on alldatasheet; now ADI)
Texas Instruments (confirmed second source: OP27A/OP27C datasheet SLOS100, first published Feb 1989, Rev E Feb 2010; an OP37G datasheet also exists)

reputation.summary: The reputation is mostly pro-audio and engineering, not 'op-amp rolling'. PMI and ADI pitched the OP27/OP37 at professional audio, with ±10 V into 600 Ω and application circuits for RIAA phono, NAB tape-head and mic preamps. A 1990s hobbyist audio FAQ says 'The OP-27, OP-37, LT1028, and LT1115 are very well received for phono preamps, head amplifiers, and microphone preamplifiers'. Douglas Self's 'The Design of Active Crossovers' (2nd ed.) has a section titled 'The OP27 Opamp'; its content was not read. The diyAudio 'a classic' quotes come from discovery notes and were not re-checked by web search. No ASR or Groner measurements were verified.
sonic_descriptors: 'nice forgotten opamp' for phono (diyAudio, via discovery notes; unverified)
'very well received' for phono, head-amp and mic preamps (1990s Atari ST diskmag audio FAQ)
typical_uses: MM phono RIAA preamps (datasheet Figure 41)
Microphone preamps, transformerless (OP37) or transformer-coupled (OP27)
Tape-head (NAB) playback preamps
Low-noise gain stages from low source impedance (<1–3 kΩ)
Precision instrumentation and ADC drivers
caveats: OP37 is decompensated and stable only at gain ≥5. An unplugged mic input (100% feedback) can oscillate.
Bias-current cancellation raises current noise, so the noise advantage disappears with high source resistance. The OP07 is better above about 3 kΩ at low frequencies.
OP27 slew rate is low (2.8 V/µs), and the 8 MHz GBW causes RIAA errors at gains above 40 dB (datasheet).
Unprotected input diodes conduct above 0.7 V differential. Use Rf ≥ 500 Ω in fast unity-gain buffers.
Best linearity with peak output current below ±10 mA (OP37 datasheet).
Single channel only; about 3 mA per amplifier.
Same part number from ADI (PMI line), ADI/LTC (OP27-LTC) and TI, with different grade sets. Specs and sound are not guaranteed identical across vendors.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OP27/OP37-specific counterfeit reports were verified. Several legitimate logos exist (PMI, ADI, LTC, TI), so a non-ADI logo alone does not mean a fake. Don't confuse OP27/OP37 with the Burr-Brown/TI OPA27/OPA37, which are different parts. Treat cheap marketplace A-grade CERDIP or TO-99 parts with suspicion. A quick check: about 3 mA supply current at ±15 V and a noise floor near 3 nV/√Hz with low source impedance.

families.name: OP275 (dual 'Butler' bipolar/JFET audio op-amp, Analog Devices)
families.tagline: ADI's audio dual with its 'Butler' bipolar+JFET input. China's classic 'warm, tube-like' op-amp and Musiland's house part; ADI says music fans rate it.
families.technology: Dual voltage-feedback op-amp with ADI's 'Butler Amplifier' input stage, which combines bipolar and JFET transistors. It is unity-gain stable. The datasheet says the design combines 'the accuracy and low noise performance of bipolar transistors, and the speed and sound quality of JFETs', and calls its 22 V/µs slew rate the fastest of any standard audio amplifier. ADI's claim that it was the first op-amp with a Butler front-end is repeated on a 1999 German product page and in EEVblog #738. The design came from the PMI (Precision Monolithics) group: the SPICE macro-models are credited 'JCB / PMI' and carry an Analog Devices copyright of 1992 and 1995. Analog Devices is the only maker; there are no second sources.

reputation.summary: OP275 was ADI's audio-targeted dual; its own datasheet pitches JFET 'sound quality'. ADI's AN-1429 (Rev. 0, David Guo) says ADI op-amps 'are reputable with music fans, like the AD797, OP275, AD8620, and ADA4627-1'. In the Chinese community (Soomal) it is the textbook 'warm, tube-like' op-amp and Musiland's signature part: Long March II (2007), MD10 (2007), Monitor 01 US and 02 US (2009), 01 PS (2010, with TPA6120), MD11 (2010), HP11 (2010/11, ahead of LME49600 buffers), MD30 (2011) and MD12 (2014, marked OP275G). In 2009 it cost nearly 20 RMB, about 20x an NE5532. Soomal's RMAA plots show a spray of low-level harmonics; Soomal links them to the warm sound but says it has no direct proof, and notes some OP275 cards sounded neutral. Other OEM uses: Denon DVD-A1 and DVD-2900, Yamaha DME32, Apogee Mini-DAC, HiFiMAN HM-602 filter stage, TempoTec DAII Plus. Japanese hobbyist rankings (nabe, Zigsow) reportedly praise a balanced, 'straight' sound; not verified.
sonic_descriptors: tube-like, valve-amp style (胆味 / 胆机风格)
warmth without losing treble (Soomal, Monitor 01 US)
typical_uses: DAC post-filter and output stage in Chinese USB DACs and sound cards (Musiland Monitor and MD series)
headphone-amp gain stage in front of a current buffer (Musiland HP11 with LME49600; Monitor 01 PS and TempoTec DAII Plus with TPA6120)
analog stages of DVD-Audio/SACD players (Denon DVD-A1, DVD-2900)
pro-audio DSP and converters (Yamaha DME32, Apogee Mini-DAC)
DAP analog filter (HiFiMAN HM-602)
op-amp rolling in socketed sound cards and motherboards
guitar pedals (a forum trace of MXR MC402 Rev E, via third-party notes)
caveats: Needs at least ±4.5 V (9 V total) supplies, so it does not suit low-voltage single-cell circuits.
Weak as a headphone driver on its own: Soomal says one OP275 cannot drive a 300 Ω HD580 with authority, so products pair it with buffers.
Measurements show a series of low-level harmonics (Soomal RMAA), so it is not a lowest-distortion choice by modern standards.
The sound depends on the implementation: Soomal found some OP275 cards neutral.
Expensive relative to NE5532/4580. Musiland used CLC2059 in the 01 Mini (2009) and MC33079 in 03 US and 03 PS (2011), but still used OP275G in the MD12 (2014).
'Warm/tube-like' is subjective community reputation; Soomal says it has no direct proof that the harmonics cause it.
Counterfeits are rumoured, but no specific report was confirmed.

families.counterfeit_notes: No concrete counterfeit report was found. The discovery hint that counterfeits 'have been reported' was not confirmed. A full-text search of 29 Soomal posts found no fake or remarked-part report. OP275 was sold in China as a premium upgrade op-amp (nearly 20 RMB in 2009, about 20x an NE5532), which is the usual profile for remarked parts. Genuine current parts are marked 'OP275G' on top. Buy OP275GPZ (DIP) or OP275GSZ (SOIC) from authorized distributors. A heuristic, not from a vendor: a relabelled NE5532/4558-class die would measure differently, so check supply current (about 2 to 2.5 mA per amplifier), slew rate (22 V/µs) and GBW (9 MHz). The GP-to-GPZ and GS-to-GSZ change is the RoHS transition, with no evidence of a die change. ADI PCN 07_0024 (mold compound) may also apply to OP275.

families.tagline: Burr-Brown's low-noise Difet (8 nV/√Hz max at 10 kHz, pA bias). TI's OPA627 datasheet calls it 'the popular OPA111', and Japanese rollers prize the metal-can OPA2111AM.
families.technology: Burr-Brown Difet (dielectrically isolated JFET-input) precision op-amp. Datasheet titles: OPA111 'Low Noise Precision Difet Operational Amplifier' (SBOS138 / PDS-526K) and OPA2111 'Dual Low Noise Precision Difet Operational Amplifier' (SBOS140 / PDS-540E). Front-page headlines for OPA111: noise 8 nV/√Hz max at 10 kHz (100% tested), bias current 1 pA max, offset 250 µV max, drift 1 µV/°C max, open-loop gain 120 dB min and CMRR 100 dB min. For OPA2111: 8 nV/√Hz max at 10 kHz and bias current 4 pA max. Burr-Brown's 1990 PSpice macromodels give GBW ≈ 2.0 MHz, SR 2 V/µs and Avol ≈ 125 dB for both parts.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part among vintage-op-amp rollers, and a well-known pA-bias, low-noise instrumentation front end. Vendor context: TI's OPA627/637 datasheet benchmarks against 'the popular OPA111'. Japan: hobby blogs praise the metal-can OPA2111AM. One reported that a swap from OPA827 gave less bass emphasis, clearer vocals and a wider soundstage; others describe a warm, analog sound. A Zigsow reviewer found the plastic OPA2111KP harder-sounding and more fatiguing than the OPA2134. China: Soomal groups OPA111 with the BB Difet parts and says OPA627/637 resolve treble much better; its 'warm, full' description applies to Difet op-amps as a class. On Head-Fi, one poster lists OPA2111KP among favourite duals. No ASR or Samuel Groner measurements were found.
sonic_descriptors: less bass emphasis, clearer vocals than OPA827 (one JP swap report)
warm, full, relaxed (Soomal, said of Difet op-amps as a class)
harder-sounding, slightly fatiguing vs OPA2134 (OPA2111KP, one Zigsow review)
typical_uses: Op-amp rolling in headphone amps (JP/CN hobbyists)
High-impedance, low-bias front ends: EEG/biopotential (the brain-duino shield uses OPA2111KP)
Current-to-voltage converters for sensors (CBA 2010 paper)
DC servo/integrator in low-noise physics preamps (arXiv physics/9902042)
Vintage preamp/phono stages (discovery note, not verified)
caveats: OPA2111 is NRND at TI, OPA2111KP is obsolete, and OPA111 is no longer available. Supply is NOS or broker stock, so remarked parts are a risk.
Slow by modern standards (about 2 MHz GBW, 2 V/µs).
TO-99 metal-can (M-suffix) parts need lead forming or an adapter to fit a DIP-8 socket.
Differences between the metal-can AM and plastic KP are grade/package differences plus forum folklore. No die change is documented.
Soomal's descriptors apply to Difet op-amps as a class.
Quiescent current, output drive and maximum supply were not verified against the datasheet.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented counterfeit reports were found. The risk is structural: OPA2111 is NRND at TI, OPA2111KP is obsolete, OPA111 is no longer available, and supply is NOS or broker stock (a 2023 broker bought KP at €18 and resold at €35). eBay 'Audio Grade' marketing and cult prices for the metal-can AM invite remarks. Practical checks (general advice, not vendor guidance): (1) Burr-Brown logo and a plausible pre-2000 date code, with marking that matches grade and package (M = TO-99, P = plastic DIP). (2) Input bias current should be low-pA (datasheet max 1 pA for OPA111 best grade, 4 pA for OPA2111). A bipolar remark (nA) or generic JFET part (tens of pA) stands out. (3) GBW should be about 2 MHz and slew about 2 V/µs, so a faster slew suggests an NE5532/TL07x-class remark.

families.name: OPA1622 (dual bipolar-input, high-output-current headphone-driver op-amp)
families.tagline: TI's 2015 dual bipolar headphone driver: 2.8 nV/rtHz, -119.2 dB THD+N at 100 mW into 32 ohms, +145/-130 mA drive. Widely used in Chinese DAPs and phones.
families.technology: Dual bipolar-input SoundPlus audio op-amp, with "Burr-Brown Audio" branding on the datasheet. It uses a single gain stage: a high-gain transconductance input stage feeding a unity-gain high-current output stage. It has a dedicated GND reference pin, to which the compensation capacitors and the enable logic are referenced, plus an EN/shutdown pin (5 uA per channel) and thermal shutdown at 175 C. It comes only in a VSON-10 (DRC) 3x3 mm package with a copper leadframe and an exposed pad that must be tied to V-.

reputation.summary: OPA1622 is a purpose-built headphone driver. It combines very low THD+N into 16-32 ohm loads, 2.8 nV/rtHz noise and high output current on 2.6 mA/ch, which suits battery gear. Teardown and review notes list it in FiiO (X7 AM3 module, X3 III, M9), Lotoo (PAW S1, Paw Gold Touch 4.4 mm output, PAW6000) and HiBy (R3 Pro II, R6 Pro Max) players, vivo Xplay6, Smartisan M1L, and Xiaomi MSM8996 phones, whose kernels carry a 'ti,opa1622' driver. DIYers built the AmpCasq integrated headamp around it (diyAudio / headphones.com). Some Japanese hobby blogs describe its sound as clear and fast, with tight bass. All community praise and device lists come from discovery notes and GitHub mirrors and were not re-verified by web search.
typical_uses: headphone output driver in DAPs, USB dongles and phones
DAC differential-to-single-ended converter plus headphone driver (TI reference design TIDUAW1, unconfirmed)
balanced (4.4 mm / 2.5 mm) headphone outputs, one device per leg
DIY integrated headamp (AmpCasq)
high-current line/buffer stage after a DAC low-pass filter
op-amp rolling on VSON-10-to-DIP-8 adapter boards (e.g. Audiophonics OPA1622 DIP8 unit)
caveats: Only available in VSON-10 3x3 mm with an exposed pad that must be soldered to V-, never ground. There is no DIP/SOIC version, so socket use needs an adapter.

Non-standard pinout with GND (pin 3) and EN (pin 8) pins, so it is not drop-in for standard dual op-amp footprints. A DIP-8 socket has no ground pin, so adapters must synthesize GND/EN. PSRR may suffer because the compensation capacitors are referenced to GND (inference from the datasheet).
EN must not float or sit on a high-Z GPIO, or the amp stays disabled. EN thresholds (0.78/0.82 V) are referenced to the GND pin. The output is NOT high-impedance in shutdown.
Output drive is limited to about +145/-130 mA. In TI's circuit that gives 150 mW into 32 ohm and 95 mW into 16 ohm before clipping, so one device per leg cannot deliver watt-class power.
Thermal: RthetaJA is 47.6 C/W and the part shuts down at 175 C, then cycles on and off while the fault persists. High rails driving low-ohm loads need copper under the pad.
Asymmetric supply ramp-up can cause audible pops. TI advises holding EN low while the rails ramp.
Minimum supply is +/-2 V.
Differential input clamp diodes (+/-0.5 V) can conduct in G=+1 circuits with fast inputs, so limit input current to 10 mA.

families.counterfeit_notes: No specific counterfeit or remarked-OPA1622 reports were found. Genuine parts are VSON-10 (DRC) with the top marking 'O1622', per the TI package addendum and alldatasheet marking page, plus the TI logo and a lot-trace code. The part ships on 250- or 3000-unit reels. The '.B' orderable suffix (OPA1622IDRCR.B) that appears in newer TI listings is a variant TI calls identical to OPA1622IDRCR, not a different die. In the hobby op-amp-rolling market it is usually pre-soldered on VSON-10-to-DIP-8 adapter boards (e.g. the iancanada adapter kit, Audiophonics 'OPA1622 Dual OPA DIP8'), where the chip cannot be inspected and GND/EN wiring varies. Buy bare parts from authorized distributors and inspect adapter boards for the O1622 marking. In 2021-era shortages OPA1622IDRCR was scarce enough that people wrote TI-store stock monitors (noxue/ticom), a typical setting for grey-market substitutes.

families.technology: True JFET input stage with a rail-to-rail output stage. Internally compensated and unity-gain stable. Rated 4.5-36 V (±2.25 to ±18 V). Internal phase-reversal protection. reputation.summary: TI's JFET-input SoundPlus family, pitched at OPA2134-class uses but with far lower datasheet distortion. Soomal describes a 'typical OPA1642 style': the whole sound is refined and balanced, with mild, delicate mids and relaxed bass. Paired with the OPA1662 (FiiO E17K) Soomal hears the 'BB' character: relaxed, grand, full dynamics, warm overall. Review sites list it as the DAC low-pass-filter or line buffer in many portable and desktop products (e.g. FiiO X3K/X3 II/X5 III/M11/E17K/K13 R2R, Lotoo PAW Gold, Astell&Kern AK380, HiBy RS6, Apogee Element 24/Groove, EarMen CH-Amp). In DIY it is the core of the 'OPA Alice' phantom-powered electret mic (Hackaday 2020), where its low quiescent current is the selling point. DIY DAC builders also pick it for its voltage-independent input capacitance. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement of the bare op-amp was checked.
sonic_descriptors: mild, fine mids (中频温和而细腻)
relaxed, grand, full dynamics, warm overall (松弛大气, 动态饱满, 偏暖; FiiO E17K with OPA1662)
typical_uses: DAC post-filter (LPF) and I/V stages in DAPs and USB DACs
line-out buffers
phantom-powered electret/condenser mic preamps (OPA Alice mic)
phono (RIAA) preamps
high-impedance piezo/guitar buffers
active filters, tone controls, mixing consoles (TI target applications)
caveats: Surface-mount only (SOIC, VSSOP, TSSOP). Op-amp rolling into DIP-8 sockets needs an adapter board (e.g. the Audiophonics OPA1642 DIP-8 adapter).
The common-mode input range stops 3.5 V below V+. Below ±3.5 V supplies it does not include midsupply, which limits low-voltage single-supply unity-gain buffers.

Not a headphone or 600 Ω driver. TI warns that 600 Ω at full supply can trip the current limit (ISC +36/-30 mA) and advises keeping output current under about 13 mA (2.8 kΩ minimum at 36 V single supply).
Capacitive-load overshoot: the datasheet recommends 24-51 Ω output isolation (Figs 19-20).
Offset is 1 mV typ / 3.5 mV max, higher than precision parts. DC-coupled outputs may need trimming or a servo.
VSSOP-8 θJA is 180 °C/W. A shorted output at ±18 V dissipates over 600 mW.
Soomal's sound descriptions are of whole devices, not the op-amp in isolation.

families.counterfeit_notes: This run's limited searches found no OPA164x-specific counterfeit reports. Two facts from the datasheet help screen parts. First, TI never offered the family in DIP, only SOIC-8 (D), VSSOP-8 (DGK), SOIC-14 and TSSOP-14, so any one-piece DIP-8 body marked OPA1642 is not a genuine TI package. Legitimate DIP-8 versions are SOIC parts on adapter boards, such as the one Audiophonics sells. Second, the genuine top markings per the 2026 TI addendum are O1641A, O1642A and O1644A on SOIC and TSSOP, and 1641 or 1642 on VSSOP, plus the TI logo and lot code. The realistic risk is remarked generic JFET duals sold on DIP adapters. Buy from authorized distributors.

reputation.summary: TI's own E2E FAQ presents the OPA1656 as the next-generation replacement for the OPA2134 and OPA2604 and calls it the lowest-voltage-noise high-voltage CMOS op-amp on the market (vendor claim). Hi-Fi and DIY users treat it as the modern, transparent, low-distortion FET-input Burr-Brown part. Community reports from the discovery sweep (not re-checked this run): in an ASR input-shorted phono noise test the roughly €5 OPA1656 matched the roughly €33 MUSES02; a Fosi ZA3 user said it 'basically wipes the floor' with Burson V7 Classic modules; Japanese listeners call it clean and balanced, with less colouration than the OPA2134; one SQ5J DAC test picked it for the I/V stage for a 'very modern' presentation; diyAudio and AMB threads discuss it as an OPA1612 substitute.
sonic_descriptors: low colouration and less harsh than OPA2134
OPA1655: high fidelity, smooth voices and instruments, slightly treble-leaning, good value (Japanese listening summary, low confidence)
typical_uses: DAC I/V and output/filter stages
headphone-amp gain and line stages (100 mA output; TI FAQ recommends it as a headphone driver)
high-gain microphone preamps (TI FAQ)
MM phono preamps (datasheet application 8.2.1; fA-level current noise suits high source impedance)
op-amp rolling on SOIC-to-DIP8 adapters (Fosi and similar)
measurement and ADC front-end buffers
active tone controls and guitar/XLR interfaces (datasheet examples)
caveats: Packages are SOIC-8 only for the OPA1656 (SOIC-8 and SOT-23-5 for the OPA1655). There is no DIP, so rolling needs third-party adapter boards of variable quality and unknown origin.

It is fast (53 MHz GBW, 20 MHz unity-gain bandwidth), so socket and adapter parasitics and poor decoupling can cause ringing or oscillation. The datasheet rates capacitive load drive at 100 pF and shows RISO of 25-50 Ω taming overshoot. The oscillation risk in sockets is an engineering inference, not a documented incident.
The marketed 2.9 nV/rtHz is measured at 10 kHz. The datasheet gives 4.3 nV/rtHz at 1 kHz and 11.8 nV/rtHz at 100 Hz (CMOS 1/f noise), so bipolar parts are quieter in low-impedance circuits.
Maximum supply is 36 V (±18 V; absolute max 40 V), so it is not a drop-in for OPA2604 circuits running ±20-24 V rails.
The input is not rail-to-rail: VCM tops out at (V+) - 2.25 V, which limits follower headroom on low rails.
Iq is 3.9 mA per channel typical (4.6 mA max), about 7.8 mA per dual package.

families.counterfeit_notes: No vendor or forensic counterfeit report was found. A Sep 2026 web search returned a general summary that AliExpress OPA1656s may be fake or may not work, and that some sellers ship genuine parts in small orders and fakes in larger ones. That summary could not be tied to a specific OPA1656 thread; the related threads are diyAudio 'OPA1612 from Aliexpress, no counterfeit but why so cheap?' and the Super-Freq 'Fake op-amps' page. Treat it as low confidence. AliExpress listings such as 'New Original Non counterfeit OPA1656IDR' exist. Vendor-documented identifiers from the SBOS901C addendum: the OPA1656 exists only in SOIC-8 (D), marked 'OP1656' plus the TI logo and lot-trace code. The OPA1655 is marked 'OP1655' in SOIC and '2R8Q' in SOT-23-5. TI makes no DIP-8 package, so every DIP 'OPA1656' is a third-party adapter; inspect the SOIC on it. Suggested plausibility checks (engineering inference): about 7.8 mA supply current per dual package at ±15-18 V; pA-level input bias current, where a relabelled bipolar part would show nA or more; 20 MHz unity-gain bandwidth and 24 V/µs slew rate.

families.name: OPA2107 (Burr-Brown/TI precision Difet JFET-input dual)
families.tagline: Burr-Brown Difet JFET dual (4.5 MHz, 18 V/us) that op-amp rollers call warm and full; HiFiMAN paired it with the OPA627 in its HM-801 and HM-901.
families.technology: Dual FET-input op-amp on Burr-Brown's proprietary dielectrically isolated (Difet) process. The datasheet says Difet keeps input bias current very low (10 pA max) without giving up offset, drift or noise. The Burr-Brown macromodel (Rev A, 10/17/90) uses a P-channel JFET input pair (.MODEL JX PJF). The datasheet and TI parametrics give 4.5 MHz GBW, 18 V/us slew and unity-gain stability. It is the faster sibling of the OPA2111 Difet dual: the 1996 EWB library gives the OPA2111 2 MHz and 2 V/us.

reputation.summary: A cult favourite from the Head-Fi op-amp-rolling era. Forum threads (Head-Fi 'OPA2107 WOW', diyAudio), Japanese blogs and Zigsow reviews reportedly call it warm, full and tube-like, placing it between the OPA2604 and OPA627. Those pages were not re-checked. Soomal (2016) puts it in a warm, full, spacious 'DiFET' sound group, a group that also covers the OPA2134 and OPA2604, and says the OPA627/637 beat it on treble resolution. Soomal's 2013 HM-901 review admits its reviewers had not heard the OPA2107 in any other device. HiFiMAN used it in the HM-801 (with OPA627), HM-602, HM-601LE and HM-901 (OPA627 + OPA2107 in the LPF). c't Lab (2007) specifies it, or an AD712, as the input amplifier of its AD16-8 ADC card, and calls it 'weit besser' (far better) than a TL072 for the 16-bit DA12-8. No independent measurements were found.
typical_uses: DAC low-pass filter (HiFiMAN HM-901, with OPA627)
DAP analogue stage (HiFiMAN HM-801, with OPA627)
Portable headphone-amp stage (HiFiMAN HM-602, HM-601LE)
Op-amp rolling in DACs and preamps (DIP-8 OPA2107AP)
Precision high-impedance instrumentation (c't Lab AD16-8 ADC input amp)
caveats: Obsolete at TI (OPA2107AP per DigiKey), so supply is now NOS or pulled stock.
Needs a fairly high supply: Tangent measured a 10.6 V minimum (OPA627: 6.8/9.8 V). The rated range is +/-4.5 V to +/-18 V.
Modest output current (about 40 mA per the models); buffer it for low-impedance headphones.
Most sonic praise is forum or blog impression, and Soomal's 'DiFET sound' group also includes non-Difet parts (OPA2134).
Counterfeit or remark risk on NOS parts is a general concern for obsolete audio op-amps; no OPA2107-specific report was verified.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA2107-specific counterfeit report was found. The part is obsolete (OPA2107AP per DigiKey), so what is sold now is NOS, pulled or broker stock, including bare die from die brokers. General checks: see whether the logo era (BB vs TI) matches the date code, and look at marking quality and package moulding. On the bench, a genuine part should show pA-level input bias current (10 pA max), about 18 V/us slew and about 4.5 MHz GBW. A remarked bipolar part will show nA-level bias current. A remarked generic JFET dual will usually be noisier than 8 nV/rtHz at 10 kHz.

families.tagline: TI's 2006 single JFET op-amp (4 nV/√Hz, 22 MHz) that DIYers treat as the modern OPA627: a DAC I/V favourite, called 'successor to the legendary stone' in a Japanese review.
families.technology: JFET-input precision voltage-feedback op-amp. Supply ±4 V to ±18 V (8 to 36 V total), abs max 40 V. Specified from -40 °C to +125 °C. Packages: SOIC-8 (D) and VSSOP/MSOP-8 (DGK). Input common-mode range and output swing are not rail-to-rail: both reach only to within 3 V of each rail. Only the single ever reached production. Early SBOS376 revisions (2006 to 2008) were titled 'OPA827, OPA2827' and announced a dual OPA2827 as Product Preview. That is why the datasheet says 'OPA827 series' and carried 'Mixed Status'. The 2013 orderables list has no OPA2827, and no evidence was found that it ever shipped. Before Rev G (Feb 2012) the datasheet also listed a high grade, OPA827I. TI's later dual in this line is OPA2828, in production since Dec 2022.

reputation.summary: Hi-Fi DIYers treat it as the cheaper modern successor to the OPA627. They use it mostly as a DAC I/V converter and in socket-rolled line and headphone stages on SOIC-to-DIP adapters. In Xonar Essence ST/STX I/V discussions it is named with LT1361, LT1028 and OPA627 as the best I/V choices. Impressions conflict. English-forum posts gathered by an earlier sweep (not re-read) call it almost neutral, clean and more dynamic and less fickle than the OPA627. A diyAudio 'Best Sounding DUAL opamps' thread describes it as bass-centric, dark, warm and laid-back, with an impressive soundstage. In Japan two Zigsow reviews carry the titles 'The strongest lineage' and 'Successor to the legendary stone', the stone being the OPA627. TI's datasheet supports audio use (-128 dB THD+N at 3 Vrms/600 Ω; 'professional audio applications'). No ASR or Samuel Groner measurement was found.
sonic_descriptors: very clean, clear and fluid (lens note)
more dynamic and less fickle than OPA627 (lens note)
bass-centric; deep, dark, warm, laid-back (diyAudio dual-opamps thread)
more assertive low end than OPA2111 (one Japanese swap report)
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) stage, e.g. socket rolling in Asus Xonar Essence ST/STX I/V positions
Portable DAC/headphone-amp op-amp swaps on DIP-8 adapters (e.g. a 2015 Fostex HP-A4 OPA827 swap blog)
Line-level buffers and preamps
Engineering (datasheet application list): 16- to 18-bit ADC drivers, DAC output buffers, transimpedance amps, filters, precision ±10 V front ends, professional audio
caveats: SMD only (SOIC-8 / VSSOP-8), so socket use needs a DIP-8 adapter. It is single channel, so a dual socket needs two parts on a 2-in-1 adapter.
Not rail-to-rail: input CM range and output swing reach only to within 3 V of each rail. On ±5 V rails usable swing is only about ±2 V.
4.8 mA typ (5.2 mA max) quiescent current per channel, and it needs at least ±4 V (8 V total).
22 MHz GBW on adapter boards: keep supply decoupling at the chip (general practice, not a documented failure report).
Listener impressions conflict (neutral/clean vs dark/warm/bass-centric). Several descriptors come from lens summaries, not first-hand re-reads.
DC precision: a PhD thesis (PatrickBaus) saw non-symmetric cubic INL with OPA827 as an ADC buffer, and a 2019 blog shows higher 1/f noise than the OPA227 near DC.
JFET bias current rises steeply with temperature (±5 nA max at 125 °C vs ±10 pA at 25 °C).
Costs much more than common audio duals.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA827-specific counterfeit or remarking report surfaced, but no search this run targeted counterfeits. Genuine TI markings per the SBOS376H package addendum (Oct 2013): SOIC-8 (D) reads 'OPA / 827 / A' plus logo and lot/date code; VSSOP-8 (DGK) reads 'NSP'. DGK lead finish may be NiPdAu or NiPdAuAg. TI has only ever listed the D and DGK packages, so a DIP-8 'OPA827' is not a genuine TI package. The OPA2827 dual never went beyond Product Preview, so any 'OPA2827' offered for sale is suspect. The part is often sold pre-soldered on adapters by marketplace sellers, and its benchmark OPA627 is among the most-faked audio op-amps. Buy from TI or authorised distributors, and check Iq (4.8 mA typ) and slew rate (at least 20 V/us).

families.name: OPA828 / OPA2828 (45 MHz, 150 V/us SiGe JFET-input, "next-generation OPA627/OPA827")
families.tagline: TI's 2018 fast JFET-input op-amp (4 nV/rtHz, 45 MHz, 150 V/us, -130 dB THD+N). DIY rollers use it on DIP adapters as a modern OPA627: extremely neutral, wide soundstage.
families.technology: JFET-input (BiFET). The datasheet says it is built on TI's "high-voltage, SiGe-complementary, JFET-bipolar process technology" (also called a "SiGe precision, high-speed, high-voltage, BiFET wafer process") and that "patented wafer processing techniques" reduce JFET gate-region noise. Offset voltage is laser-trimmed at two temperatures; offset drift and quiescent current are also trimmed. It has a proprietary slew-boost circuit that fires on large input differential voltage, plus an overload power limiter that turns slew-boost off after about 300 ns. There are no anti-parallel diodes across the inputs ('MUX-friendly'), so the differential input can reach the full supply, but the inputs are diode-clamped to the rails. It is specified at G=+1 (57 deg phase margin with CL=30 pF). The output is not rail-to-rail in practice (0.9 V typ / 1.2 V max from each rail at 10 kohm), even though some distributor blurbs label it 'RRO'.

part_numbers.notes: SOIC-8 (D), tube of 75. Top marking 'OPA828'. D-package spec set. Pins 1, 5 and 8 are NC; there are no offset-null pins. Shown as Active in both the 17-Jun-2025 and 9-Nov-2025 package addenda of SBOS671D. The original 2018 package. Covered by PCN20221117006 (Nov 2022): a datasheet specification change only, with no device or marking change.

SOIC-8 (D), 2500-piece tape and reel. Marking 'OPA828'. Mouser P/N 595-OPA828IDR appears in the Mouser field of the stefaweb Q17-Mini-3.0 and Q17-TURBO-2.0 KiCad schematics. Covered by PCN20221117006 (a spec change only).
SOIC-8 (D) tube, G4 orderable variant. Marking 'OPA828'. Active per the 2025 addenda. It is not named in the PCN20221117006 search summary (only ID and IDR are).

HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN): 2500 on T&R (R) or 250 on T&R (T). Top marking '2RAJ'. Added as preview in Rev C (Oct 2022) and moved to production in Rev D (Dec 2022). Has its own, tighter DC spec set (Vos, drift, Ib) but a lower CMRR than the D package.

The dual exists only in HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN); SBOS671D lists no SOIC or DIP dual (web-confirmed). Top marking '2QGJ'. Standard dual pinout (OUT A=1, V-=4, OUT B=7, V+=8). The pad is isolated (>10 Mohm) from the die; TI says to solder it and tie it to V- or GND. It has its own product folder (ti.com/product/OPA2828). It first appears in Rev C (preview) and reached production in Rev D (Dec 2022).

reputation.summary: DIY and op-amp-rolling hobbyists treat the OPA828 as the modern high-speed successor to the OPA627, matching TI's 'next generation OPA627 and OPA827' positioning. A long diyAudio thread, 'OPA828 / OPA2828 vs OPA627' (at least 7 pages), is web-confirmed. In it one user calls the OPA2828 extremely neutral, with a very wide soundstage, very transparent, with lots of micro-detail and no harshness, and rates it above the OPA1642. Another calls the OPA828 completely transparent and fatigue-free over a full day. A third reports no oscillation in any circuit tried, including breadboards. The thread also notes that OPA627 fans may hear the OPA2828 as 'thin'. These are individual forum opinions, not a consensus measurement. Audiophonics sells an 'OPA828 Dual OPA DIP8' adapter unit for rolling. Japanese 2026 roundups (maimai-audio), which use descriptors such as elegant, low-colour and spacious, were not re-verified. GitHub-verified uses: the open-source Q17 power amplifier switched U1 from OPA1641 to OPA828 'for JFET lovers'; a Japanese DIY board (indare/pcb_work) uses two singles on a DIP module; a 2025 instrumentation project chose it over the OPA627/637 on price (~$7 vs ~$30). The datasheet gives -130 dB THD+N and 137 dB CCIF IMD. No independent ASR or Samuel Groner measurement was located.
sonic_descriptors: doesn't hurt the ears / no listening fatigue
typical_uses: DAC I/V conversion and post-filter / output stages
line buffers and preamps
RIAA phono preamps
headphone amps with a separate buffer (OPA828 + LME49600)
power-amplifier input/error-amp stage (Q17 amplifier)
op-amp rolling on SOIC-to-DIP adapter modules (e.g. Audiophonics 'OPA828 Dual OPA DIP8' unit; two singles on a dual-DIP adapter, or OPA2828 on a PowerPAD-capable adapter)
caveats: No DIP package exists. The single comes in SOIC-8 or HVSSOP-8 and the dual only in HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD, so socketed use needs adapter boards, which add parasitics. TI says to solder the DGN exposed pad and tie it to V- or GND.

This is a fast part (45 MHz GBW, 150 V/us, 57 deg phase margin at CL=30 pF). TI says to isolate heavier capacitive loads with a small series resistor (e.g. 50 ohm). Layout, decoupling and adapter parasitics matter. The indare/pcb_work review puts it in its 'layout-sensitive' group, well below LT1364, and rates it relatively well-behaved. A diyAudio user reports no oscillation, even on breadboards.

Slew-boost engages when the inputs are driven far apart. TI warns this 'can distort the signal' and advises keeping the inputs close together where low distortion is needed (relevant to clipping and overload, not normal linear closed-loop use).

Minimum supply is +/-4 V (8 V). Common-mode range is only (V-)+2.5 V to (V+)-3.5 V, and the output needs 0.9 V typ (1.2 V max) of headroom from each rail. Despite 'RRO' in some distributor blurbs, it is not rail-to-rail and is unsuitable for 5 V or low-voltage portable gear. TI E2E notes the swing spec is a 'slam' test; the linear range is the one given with the AOL spec.

It draws 5.5 mA per channel (about 165 mW/ch at +/-15 V), which gives a self-rise of roughly 20 C with the SOIC RthJA of 121.5 C/W. JFET bias current rises steeply with temperature (max +/-400 pA at 0-85C, +/-3 nA at 125C). A two-single adapter draws about 11 mA.
Output current is +/-30 mA linear (50 mA short-circuit). That is fine for 600 ohm and above, but it is not a stand-alone low-impedance headphone driver.
The inputs have no anti-parallel protection diodes. Differential input up to the supply is allowed, but the inputs are diode-clamped to the rails, so limit input current to 10 mA.
Datasheet limits for OPA828ID/IDR changed under PCN20221117006 (Nov 2022, spec-only, same device). Do not compare Rev B (2018-2022) limits with Rev C/D limits as if the silicon had changed.

revision_history.changes: Initial release, probably advance information (inferred). Changes not listed in the current history.
Not itemised in SBOS671D, whose history starts at A->B.

'First release of production-data data sheet'. Single OPA828 in SOIC-8 only, D-package typicals 50 uV, 0.45 uV/C, 1 pA, and 'Seismic Test Equipment' among the applications. Its SOIC limits predate the PCN20221117006 specification change.

A datasheet specification change for OPA828ID/OPA828IDR 'to accurately reflect device characteristics'. Spec change only: no device change and no change to fit, form, function, quality, reliability or product identification. The affected parameters were not identified in this pass. It falls between Rev C (Oct 2022) and Rev D (Dec 2022).

B->C per TI: added OPA828 and OPA2828 in the DGN (HVSSOP, 8) preview package 'and associated content'; added the TA symbol and a table note in Recommended Operating Conditions; deleted VS and TA from Electrical Characteristics; changed a section title from 'Capacitive Load and Stability' to 'Noise Performance'; added the missing Equation 2; added a 'PowerPAD Design Considerations (DGN Package Only)' section. The log does not itemise SOIC limit changes, but PCN20221117006 shows that OPA828ID/IDR limits did change around this time. The package-split rows (DGN tighter Vos/drift/Ib, lower CMRR) presumably arrived here (inferred).

Changed OPA828 and OPA2828 in the DGN package from preview to production data and added associated content (current revision, web-confirmed). TI's heading says 'Revision C (December 2018)' while the Rev C entry says October 2022 (apparently a TI typo). The PDF is regenerated with new addenda (2025-07-26 and 2026-08-11 builds) under the same letter.

A macro-model referencing SBOS671B. 1.1: C14 fix; Aol, GBW and phase margin, CLAW, Isc, Vos and drift updated. 1.2: IQ_SRC direction fix. 1.3: R_NOISELESS .model moved into the subckt and the symbol updated. Simulation-model changes only.

silicon_changes.when: November 2022 (PCN20221117006), coinciding with SBOS671C (Oct 2022) / SBOS671D (Dec 2022)
silicon_changes.identification: No marking or orderable change: TI states there are no changes to product identification. Parts cannot be told apart physically. Only the datasheet revision differs: SBOS671B (Dec 2018) or earlier gives the old limits; SBOS671C/D gives the revised limits.
silicon_changes.summary: 'Same part number, different datasheet' hazard, not a die change. TI's PCN20221117006 announced a specification change for the SOIC OPA828ID/IDR 'to accurately reflect device characteristics', with no expected impact on fit, form, function, quality or reliability and no device change. SOIC limits in Rev C/D therefore differ from Rev B in at least one parameter, which was not identified in this pass. A 2019 TI E2E thread titled 'OPA828: Output swing specification disagrees with datasheet figures' may be related (unconfirmed).

spec_deltas.parameter: OPA828ID/IDR datasheet limits (specific parameters not identified)

silicon_changes.audio_impact: None expected: the silicon is unchanged, and noise, GBW, slew rate and THD+N typicals appear the same in the Rev-B-era text and Rev D. The only practical risk is a design-margin check against old Rev B limits.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: low - it is a spec-only PCN with the same device and markings. Re-check worst-case budgets only if a design was qualified against the Rev B limit table.

silicon_changes.when: October 2022 (preview, SBOS671C) / December 2022 (production, SBOS671D)
silicon_changes.identification: Orderable suffix DGN (HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD) vs D (SOIC-8). Top marking '2RAJ' (OPA828 DGN) or '2QGJ' (OPA2828 DGN) vs 'OPA828' (SOIC). The spec rows first appear in datasheet Rev C/D.
silicon_changes.summary: A package extension, not a documented die change. TI added a thermally enhanced DGN package for the single and introduced the dual OPA2828 in DGN only (web-confirmed). DGN parts carry a separate, tighter DC spec set than the SOIC OPA828. TI does not say that a new die, process or fab is involved, and no DGN-specific PCN was found. The SOIC part is the same device, but its datasheet limits were revised at the same time (see PCN20221117006). Whether the DGN part uses revised silicon or only a different trim, test or package flow is unknown. AC specs (noise, GBW, slew rate, THD+N) are common to both packages.

spec_deltas.parameter: Input bias and offset current typ / max @25C
spec_deltas.after: DGN: +/-0.2 pA / +/-5 pA (front page says 0.1 pA)

silicon_changes.audio_impact: Negligible for audio. The deltas are DC precision and a few dB of CMRR; noise, GBW, slew rate and THD+N are specified identically. The DGN runs cooler because of the PowerPAD. The dual needs a PowerPAD-capable adapter.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: low - different footprints, suffixes and markings mean the parts cannot be confused. Only the OPA2828 is restricted to HVSSOP-8, with an exposed pad that should be soldered.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA828 or OPA2828 counterfeits were documented in the sources found. This pass's six web searches did not target counterfeits, so the question is open either way. Authenticity facts from TI's 2025 package addenda: (1) TI makes no DIP-8 version of either part, so any 'OPA828'/'OPA2828' DIP is an adapter board (e.g. Audiophonics' 'OPA828 Dual OPA DIP8' unit); a DIP-8 IC body laser-marked OPA828/OPA2828 is not a TI package. (2) The OPA2828 exists only in HVSSOP-8 (DGN), marked '2QGJ', so an SOIC-8 or DIP body marked 'OPA2828' is suspect. (3) A genuine SOIC OPA828 is marked 'OPA828' and a DGN OPA828 '2RAJ'. The OPA627 it replaces in rolling circles is heavily counterfeited. The OPA828 is much cheaper (~$7 vs ~$30 for OPA627/637 per a 2025 project note), which lowers the incentive to fake it, but adapter modules are usually bought from marketplaces. Inspect the chip marking and, where possible, check slew rate (~150 V/us) and pA-level bias current.

families.name: OPA211 / OPA2211 (1.1 nV/√Hz bipolar precision, single / dual)
families.tagline: TI's 1.1 nV/√Hz, 45 MHz (G = 1) bipolar precision op-amp. Head-Fi rollers found the OPA2211A more open than the LM4562, and Shanling product copy lists it in DAC low-pass stages.
families.technology: Bipolar-input precision voltage-feedback op-amp. It is unity-gain stable, has a rail-to-rail output and back-to-back differential input protection diodes, and its EMI rejection (EMIRR) is characterized. It runs on 4.5–36 V. On the single OPA211, pin 8 is Shutdown (active high) in the VSSOP (DGK) and SON (DRG) packages and NC in SOIC-8 (D). The commercial dual comes only in SMD packages: SO-8 PowerPAD (DDA) and 3×3 mm SON (DRG). TI does not name the fab process.

reputation.summary: A well-regarded modern bipolar part for rolling and for DAC output stages. The evidence is forum and blog impressions (read through search summaries), not published measurements. Head-Fi rollers preferred the OPA211 to most other parts, including the LM/LME chips. One Head-Fi post found the OPA2211A 'more open, yet not harsh' in the highs than the LM4562, with a 'natural roundness and warmth'. One listener found female vocals a bit 'creamy'. Japanese reviewers call the OPA2211 versatile, with resolution and power in balance and a wider sense of space. They find it clearer than the OPA2134 and drier than the OPA627. A zigsow review says it suits some genres better than others. On the SQ5J DAC blog, an OPA1656 I/V stage followed by an OPA2211 differential stage gave a 'very modern' sound. Third-party retail copy of Shanling products (mirrored on GitHub) lists the OPA2211 in the M6 Pro 21 LPF, the EM7 LPF and an OPA2211+BD139/BD140 amplifier stage. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement was checked (not searched in this pass).
typical_uses: DAC differential / summing and low-pass filter stages
DAC post-filter in Shanling products (M6 Pro 21 LPF; EM7 LPF and amp stage, per third-party retail copy)
headphone-amp and DAC op-amp rolling via SOIC/PowerPAD-to-DIP adapters
low-impedance, low-noise gain stages: sources below ~2 kΩ per TI, ADC drivers, and SR560-style LNAs as a unity-gain-stable stand-in for the OP37/LT1028
caveats: SMD only. The dual comes in SO-8 PowerPAD (DDA) or SON-8, so a DIP socket needs an adapter. The datasheet says the exposed pad 'must be connected to V–' (not ground), and soldering it improves heat dissipation and gives specified performance. On the single SON it is 'required'. Check how the adapter connects the pad.

On the VSSOP and SON singles, pin 8 is Shutdown (active high). The datasheet says it 'must be connected to a valid high or low voltage or driven, and not left open-circuit'. Rev L shows pin 8 as NC on the SOIC-8 single, so a SOIC single on a standard adapter is safe.
Rev H of the datasheet (Nov 2015) had the SON single's V+ and V− pin numbers swapped; rev I (June 2016) fixed it. Do not lay out a SON board from a rev H copy.
The back-to-back differential input diodes can conduct on fast, large steps at G = 1. Input current must then be limited to 10 mA, and the series resistor that does this adds noise.

Current noise is 1.7 pA/√Hz. TI (SBOS377L §8.1.3) positions the OPAx211 for source impedances below 2 kΩ. It suggests the OPA227 for 10–100 kΩ and a FET part such as the OPA132 above 100 kΩ. The OPA828 datasheet (Fig. 7-7) makes the same comparison against the OPA828.
It is a wideband part (45 MHz at G = 1), and the datasheet gives an overshoot-vs-capacitive-load curve, so layout and decoupling on adapters matter. Community reports of oscillation were not checked.
Listening impressions depend on genre and circuit (zigsow; Head-Fi notes that op-amp 'sound' is circuit-specific).

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit reports were checked (not searched), so this is not a clean bill. Vendor facts that help spot odd parts (rev L and the 9-Nov-2025 addendum): no DIP package is listed. The OPA2211A comes only as SO-8 PowerPAD (DDA, top marking 'OPA 2211 A', NiPdAu, MSL1) or 3×3 mm SON (marking 'OBHQ'). The SOIC single is marked 'OPA 211' (high grade) or 'OPA 211 A'. In VSSOP ('OBCQ') and SON ('OBDQ') both grades share one marking, so the grade cannot be read from the part. Any 'OPA2211' in a DIP-8 body is an adapter module or a remarked part. A DDA body with no exposed pad on its underside would also be suspect (inference from the package definition). Buy from authorized distributors, and on adapter modules check that the pad is soldered to V− (the datasheet says it 'must be connected to V–').

families.name: OPA227 / OPA228 (OPA2227 / OPA2228 / OPA4227 / OPA4228)
families.tagline: Burr-Brown's 3 nV/rtHz precision bipolar successor to OP27/OP37 and Tangent's PIMETA default; the decompensated OPA2228 is prized for resolution.
families.technology: Bipolar, precision low-noise, laser-trimmed, with input bias-current cancellation and back-to-back differential input clamp diodes. OPA227 is unity-gain stable (8 MHz, 2.3 V/us). OPA228 is decompensated for G>=5 (33 MHz, 10 V/us on TI's product page; 11 V/us typ in the Rev A table). The singles have offset trim on pins 1/8 (OP-27 compatible) in Rev A, and datasheet text surfaced in 2026 searches still describes pins 1/8 trim. No trim-to-NC change was found for this family, unlike OPA132/OPA627.

Copies in the old Burr-Brown layout survive on Octopart (OPA4227UA Burr-Brown), CERN and kontest.ru, but their revision letters were not identified. The datasheet positions the OPA227 as a replacement for OP-27, LT1007 and MAX427, and the OPA228 for OP-37, LT1037 and MAX437. TI took over after acquiring Burr-Brown. Datasheet revisions: SBOS110A (January 2005), SBOS110B (June 2015) and SBOS110C (November 2022). TI product pages list Rev. C as current (Sep 2026). TI's OPA228 macromodel is dated Rev. A 04/19/02. The 2022 PSpice models (June 2022) were updated 'as per the datasheet'. No second sources are known.

reputation.summary: Tangent (tangentsoft) made the OPA2227 the default op-amp for his PIMETA amp. He described it as sounding very like the OPA132/OPA134, minus the bass bloom. He found the decompensated OPA228 more resolving and 'lively' than the OPA132, but it oscillated in his low-gain CMoy, so he preferred the OPA227. On Head-Fi the OPA2227 divides opinion: some users call it 'horribly dull and laid back', while others call the OPA2228 'waaaay better' and 'pleasant sounding', provided gain is 5 or more or the part is compensated. Japanese C-Area wiki rates the OPA2228 as flat, high-resolution, smooth and realistic. It describes the OPA2227 as OPA2134-like but leaning to the low end (Zigsow: 'bass stands out'). No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were located. These are subjective community impressions, not measurements.
sonic_descriptors: neutral, OPA132/OPA134-like without bass bloom (Tangent, OPA227)
flat, high resolution, smooth continuity, realistic (C-Area wiki, OPA2228)
more lively and resolving than OPA132 (Tangent, OPA228)
typical_uses: CMoy / PIMETA headphone amplifiers (DIP-8 OPA2227PA / OPA2228PA)
DAC output / line stages and preamps with low source impedance (datasheet: best below ~20 kohm source)
Op-amp rolling in socketed DIP-8 audio gear
Professional audio equipment (named in datasheet applications)
Low-noise reference / supply buffering in DIY DACs, e.g. OPA2227 buffering a 2.5 V reference in a diyAudio DAC project
caveats: OPA228/OPA2228 is decompensated (G>=5). It can oscillate in unity- or low-gain sockets or with capacitive load. The datasheet recommends a feedback capacitor CF for G=+2/-2, which raises output noise.
Back-to-back input clamp diodes: large fast input steps in a follower can drive destructive current. The datasheet limits input current to 20 mA, and 'subtle damage' can shift offset and noise.
Not rail-to-rail. Output needs about 2 V headroom (3.5 V into 600 ohm) and Isc is about 45 mA, so it is marginal from a 9 V battery into low-impedance headphones without a buffer.
Input bias current is cancelled internally; TI says a bias-balancing resistor raises offset and noise and is not recommended.
Iq about 3.7 mA per amplifier, which matters for battery life.
A-grade vs non-A grade differs only in DC precision, which is irrelevant for audio (Tangent).

families.technology: BiFET: JFET-input op amp with bipolar gain and output stages. Offset and drift are set by laser wafer trimming. Internally compensated and unity-gain stable. reputation.summary: The AD712 was a mainstream 'better' audio dual in the late 1980s and 1990s. The rec.audio FAQ (v1.5, June 1993, from an archived text file) lists it among the better op amps for audio, next to NE5532, LM833, AD827 and OPA2604. ADI marketed the AD711/AD712 as enhanced replacements for the LF411/TL081 and LF412/TL082, so DIYers used the AD712 as a drop-in upgrade in TL072/TL082 sockets. Its strengths are 0.0003% THD, 120 dB crosstalk, 20 V/µs slew and pA bias, which suit high-impedance line stages and filters. It is now a tier-C legacy part, overtaken by lower-noise JFET parts. The discovery claims about CD-player use and Walt Jung's ADI-era writing were not web-verified. No modern measurements and no verified sonic descriptors were collected.
typical_uses: Drop-in TL072/TL082/LF412 upgrade in CD-player and DAC output/filter stages (DIY practice; attributed to forum sources)
High-impedance line buffers and active filters (the data sheet includes second-order and 9-pole Chebyshev filter examples)
DAC/ADC buffers and I/V stages that need fast settling (the data sheet shows AD565A/AD7545 settling examples)
Photodiode and electrometer preamps (pA bias, with guarding)
caveats: Voltage noise of 18 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz is high next to bipolar parts (NE5532, OP27) and modern JFETs (OPA1642, OPA827). It is a poor choice for low-impedance or MM-phono inputs.
Output phase reversal if either input goes more negative than about -14.1 V at ±15 V supplies. The CM range reaches only -11.5 V (data sheet footnote).
Needs at least ±4.5 V supplies and is not rail-to-rail.
Output is about 25 mA. It is not a headphone driver.
Loads above about 1500 pF need a 100 Ω isolation resistor (data sheet Figure 46).
JFET bias current doubles every 10 °C. Hot chassis raise bias and offset errors in DC-coupled designs.
Pinout is the standard single (AD711) / dual (AD712) / quad (AD713). Check the pinout before swapping parts.

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit AD711/712/713 parts have been documented. The risk runs the other way: fake OPA627s. The ZeptoBars decap (2014, covered by Hackaday) found an AD744 die under an OPA627 marking. Users in the Head-Fi thread 'fake opa627's in the wild' also report remarked AD711-type parts sold as OPA627, with about 18 kΩ measured between pins as a check. That report is forum-level only (low confidence). Electrical clues: an AD711-class die slews about 20 V/µs, against about 55 V/µs for the OPA627. It also draws far less supply current (AD712 Rev. I: 5.0 mA typ for two amplifiers). Data sheets before Rev. D (9/2001) carried a metallization photograph, which helps when comparing decapped dies. Buy from authorised distributors; current PDIP/SOIC production carries the Z (RoHS) suffix.

families.technology: BiFET: JFET input differential pair (p-channel JFETs in ADI's macro-models) with bipolar gain and output stages. Single op amp. AD743 is unity-gain stable (4.5 MHz, 2.8 V/us). reputation.summary: More of an instrumentation legend than a mainstream op-amp-rolling part. It pairs 2.9 nV/rtHz voltage noise with only 6.9 fA/rtHz current noise, so it stays quiet with both low and very high source impedances. That makes it a reference choice for hydrophone, piezo and charge-amplifier front ends and for low-noise measurement. For example, Rubiola chose the AD743 for AM-noise detector amplifiers. Discovery notes report a niche following in MM phono/RIAA stages and high-impedance mic or piezo preamps; this was not web-verified. Community sound descriptors and measurements were not retrieved.
typical_uses: MM phono / RIAA preamp input stage (niche following; per discovery notes, not web-verified)
Hydrophone and piezo-film charge amplifiers (e.g. AD745 charge amp for PVDF film in a Taiwanese thesis)
Low-noise measurement front ends (AM/phase-noise detector amplifiers, Rubiola arXiv:physics/0512082)
Cryogenic bolometer readout / precision bias circuits (AD743 in arXiv physics/9902042)
High-impedance sensor and accelerometer preamps
caveats: Single op amp only: not a drop-in for dual (5532/TL072-style) DIP-8 sockets. It needs two parts per stereo pair plus an adapter.
The surface-mount part is a 16-lead wide SOIC (R-16), not SOIC-8, so an adapter or custom footprint is needed.
AD745 compensation is optimized for higher gains (data sheet). It is not a unity-gain buffer. The exact minimum stable gain (believed 5) is unconfirmed.
Large JFET input capacitance (20 pF in the model) creates a feedback pole with high-value resistors, so a feedback capacitor may be needed.
About 8 mA quiescent current per amplifier (model), high for a JFET op amp.
Minimum supply is about +/-4.8 V; not a 5 V single-supply part.
Several SOIC reel and leaded variants were discontinued via ADI PDNs, so check which orderable part numbers remain active.

families.counterfeit_notes: No AD743/AD745-specific counterfeit reports were found (forums not searched). Generic risk: expensive single JFET op amps are remarking targets. Checks: (1) supply current should be about 8 mA per amp at +/-15 V, while a remarked TL071-class part draws far less and is much noisier. (2) The documented surface-mount package is the 16-lead SOIC (R-16), so treat an 'AD743/AD745' in SOIC-8 with suspicion. (3) Several R-16 reel and leaded variants were discontinued (ADI PDN 14_0014), so a 'new' leaded AD745KR-16 offered today is old stock at best. (4) Buy from ADI or authorised distributors.

reputation.summary: A niche part for Hi-Fi hobbyists. ADI itself pitched the AD744 for demanding audio applications (0.0003% THD, 13 MHz GBW) and as a fast-settling buffer for 12/14-bit DACs and ADCs. Tangent's CMoy op-amp survey (read via the Soomal translation) measured the AD744: $4.52 at Digi-Key, minimum supply 6.8 V for 0.5 V into 33 ohms; no listening verdict was found. Its main notoriety is as the donor die in counterfeit OPA627s (ZeptoBars, April 2014, covered by Hackaday, Head-Fi and diyAudio). The discovery note calling it a '1990s DIY I/V favourite' has no primary community source.
typical_uses: Fast-settling buffers for 12/14-bit DACs and ADCs (ADI positioning)
Audio stages (ADI marketing cites 0.0003% THD)
DAC I/V and line stages (discovery note; not verified)
Precision current drivers and instrumentation
caveats: The AD744's compensation pin has no counterpart on the OPA627 (ZeptoBars), so it is not a clean pin-for-pin OPA627 substitute. Check the pin function before op-amp rolling.
Noise is about 3x the OPA627's (ZeptoBars); ADI's LTspice model uses ~16 nV/rtHz.
Offset is higher than the OPA627's (0.5 mV vs 0.1 mV, per ZeptoBars).
Weaker headphone driver in Tangent's table (6.8 V needed for 0.5 V into 33 ohms).
Some order codes are obsolete (AD746JRZ-REEL).
