families.counterfeit_notes: No fakes sold as AD744 were found. The hazard runs the other way: genuine AD744 dies have been remarked as OPA627. In April 2014 ZeptoBars decapped a cheap eBay DIP 'OPA627' (about $2 per Hackaday; $2.70 with shipping per the Habr text). It held an ADI AD744 die with only one laser-trimmed resistor, against several on a genuine metal-can OPA627. ZeptoBars thought a Chinese packager had bought AD744 dies or wafers; ADI's datasheet lists chip (die) form. The AD744's frequency-compensation feature was unused because the OPA627 has no matching pin. The 'AD'/'B744' die markings come from the Habr text and were not re-confirmed here. How to spot an AD744-based fake: (1) about 3x the noise and higher offset (0.5 mV vs 0.1 mV) than a genuine OPA627; (2) lower supply current, 3.5 mA for the AD744 (ADI datasheet) against about 7 mA for the OPA627 (TI figure, not re-checked here); (3) a decap. Discussed on Hackaday, Head-Fi and diyAudio ('more fake eBay semis (OPA627=AD744)'). Buy genuine AD744/AD746 through authorized distribution.

families.name: AD8022 (ADI dual high-speed, low-noise op-amp)
families.technology: Dual high-speed, low-noise bipolar op-amp (datasheet title: 'Dual High Speed, Low Noise Op Amp'), high output current

reputation.summary: Posters in Head-Fi's 'The Opamp thread' say replacing the NJM4580 with the AD8022 improved resolution and timbre accuracy, and that it sounds close to the AD797ANZ. They describe it as spatial, clear and very transparent ('pure music'), and say it can drive headphones directly. Caveats: it needs careful decoupling or it oscillates, and its high input bias current makes it poor for high-impedance inputs.

families.name: AD825 (single high-speed JFET-input op amp)
families.tagline: A cheap, fast single JFET op amp (41 MHz, 125 V/us, 12 nV/rtHz). DIY op-amp rollers call it punchy and rich, and LC Audio sold it as an upgrade part.
families.technology: A single JFET-input, high-speed, voltage-feedback op amp from Analog Devices. ADI's SPICE macro-model (JCH / ADI Central Apps, 1999) uses a P-channel JFET differential input pair. The datasheet specifies it fully at +/-5 V and +/-15 V. The orderables found are SOIC-8 and a 16-lead wide SOIC (R-16); the R-16 was added in datasheet Rev. F (10/04). No dual or quad version exists.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part from the mid-2000s op-amp-rolling era. Head-Fi users call it punchy and intimate, with a rich timbre and thick texture that suits female vocals and strings; one fan of 2x AD825 on an adapter says 'AD825 is the best'. Others hear it as flat or unemotional in some DACs, or as more coloured and a bit closed-in than the AD797. The LME49990 was reported as smoother, with a firmer low end. LC Audio Technology sold AD825 upgrade parts. Audio Asylum and diyAudio threads reportedly suggest it as a better replacement for the AD712 in the Parasound HCA-2200 MK-I input stage. No objective audio measurements were found. All sonic claims are forum opinion.
sonic_descriptors: good for female voices and strings
flat / unemotional in some DACs (dissenting view)
coloured and a bit closed-in compared with the AD797 (dissenting view)
less smooth, lighter low end than the LME49990 (comparison)
typical_uses: Op-amp rolling in DAC and CD-player analog stages, on SOIC-to-DIP adapters (two AD825s per dual socket)
Drop-in upgrade for AD711/AD712-class JFET op amps (forum discussion, e.g. Parasound HCA-2200 MK-I)
Headphone amplifiers (Tangentsoft / Head-Fi)
LC Audio Technology upgrade kits
caveats: Single-channel and surface-mount only (SOIC-8 / SOIC-16). Replacing a DIP dual needs an adapter carrying two chips.
It is a 41 MHz part, so adapter wiring and local decoupling matter (general high-speed practice; no AD825-specific oscillation reports were found).
It needs more supply headroom to swing 2 V into 330 ohm than parts such as the AD823 (8.6 V vs 6.1 V minimum in the Tangentsoft test).
The praise is subjective forum opinion. No published THD+N measurements were found. The forum sources were not re-checked in this pass.

No DIP-8 or dual version was found, though the ordering guides of Rev. A and Rev. C were not read. reputation.summary: This is a niche op-amp for rolling in CD players, not a mainstream audio legend. ADI designed it for video, CATV, copiers, LCDs, scanners and fax machines. In the Audio Asylum 'tweaks' forum and on diyAudio, a few users who swapped it into CD-player output and I/V stages called the sound 'much cleaner, more open, and more detailed'. They also reported more precise instrument placement than the AD827, and one Audio Asylum poster found it 'almost as good' as the OPA637. Its appeal is video-class speed (50 MHz, 350 V/µs) combined with stability into capacitive loads. No independent measurements (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner) were found. A 2005 translation of Tangent's op-amp notes (DiyEden/Soomal) put the AD826 on its list to test, but no review followed.
typical_uses: CD-player analog output stage op-amp swap
DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) converter
Video and line drivers (the designed use)
Buffers driving cables or capacitive loads
caveats: The evidence is thin: a few forum posts from the discovery notes, which were not re-read in this pass. There are no published measurements.

This is a 50 MHz video part. Tight decoupling and short leads are sensible when socket-rolling, although ADI rates it stable into any capacitive load. This is engineering inference, not a reported failure.
Input bias current is high (3.3 µA typ, 6.6 µA max), which can cause DC offset with large feedback or source resistances.
Voltage noise is moderate at 15 nV/√Hz, well above NE5532- or AD797-class parts.
It draws up to 15 mA per package (7.5 mA max per amplifier), so it runs warmer and drains batteries faster than audio duals.
The DIP versions (AD826AN/ANZ) are reportedly discontinued, so DIP socket-rollers depend on old stock or SOIC-to-DIP adapters.
The Tangent/DiyEden headphone-amp notes argued that ultra-high-speed op-amps are generally a poor fit for simple headphone amps.

families.name: AD843 (34 MHz CBFET JFET-input single op-amp)
families.tagline: ADI's 34 MHz, 250 V/us CBFET single op-amp. A DiyEden/Soomal headphone-amp study called it the only rival to the OPA627, and smoother; Head-Fi opinion is split.
families.technology: Fast-settling JFET-input single op-amp on ADI's CBFET process. The ADI data sheet is titled '34 MHz, CBFET Fast Settling Op Amp': 34 MHz bandwidth, 250 V/us slew rate, 135 ns settling to 0.01% for a 10 V step, 0.6 nA input bias current. ADI's SPICE macro-model (Rev. A, 1/92) uses a p-channel JFET input pair, with the dominant pole at about 1.23 kHz and about 10.7 mA typical supply current. Single channel only; ADI never made a dual AD843. Packages: 8-lead plastic DIP (N-8), 16-pin SOIC (R-16), cerdip (Q) and metal can (H).

reputation.summary: A niche cult part with split opinion. DiyEden published a Chinese translation of an English headphone-amp op-amp study on Soomal (2005). It quotes an article called 'The best op-amp I've heard' naming the AD843 the only op-amp that can rival the OPA627. The author found it smoother than the OPA627, trading some resolution for smoothness, with 'boldness, charm, vitality and passion'. A pair cost about half as much as a pair of OPA627s. The same study rates the AD845 as less detailed and says to upgrade to the AD843, and rates the AD8610 as having more detail and smoothness than the AD843. Head-Fi opinion (from an earlier search summary, not re-checked) is largely negative: 'harsh and unpleasant', 'no competition for OPA637', 'stay away from this - bad offset, oscillation, etc.'. One user found 2x AD843JN on an adapter 'really good' but warm, because of the high quiescent current. It also appears in Maverick TubeMagic D1 op-amp rolling lists. No objective measurements (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: bold / energetic ('气魄、神韵、活力和热情')
typical_uses: headphone amplifier op-amp rolling (CMoy-style, single-channel sockets)
DAC output stage rolling, used in pairs on dual adapters
replacement for OPA627 in single sockets
caveats: High quiescent current: 13 mA max per the data sheet, about 10.7 mA typical in ADI's model. It runs warm and is poor for battery amps.
Needs a high supply voltage: hobbyist-measured minimums of 8.2 V and 12.2 V. The sound degrades quickly as the supply voltage drops.
Head-Fi reports of bad offset and oscillation. It is a 34 MHz, 250 V/us part, so it is sensitive to layout and decoupling.
Single only: dual-socket use needs two chips on an adapter.
The surface-mount version is a 16-pin SOIC (R-16), not an SO-8, so it does not fit standard SO-8 adapters.

families.counterfeit_notes: No reports of fake AD843s were found, but this was not searched specifically. Generic caution: DIP AD843JN/KN parts sold on marketplaces are likely relabelled or pulled parts. Check the ADI logo style and date code. Measure quiescent current: roughly 10-13 mA is expected (13 mA data-sheet max, about 10.7 mA model typical). A much lower Iq points to a substituted die such as a TL071-class part. Also check the offset against the grade limits: 2 mV for J, 1 mV for K. A genuine SOIC part is a 16-pin R-16 package; an 8-pin SOIC marked AD843 is suspect.

reputation.summary: A niche ADI JFET single with thin enthusiast coverage. The only located listening report is a Chinese translation (DiyEden, on Soomal, 2005) of a headphone-amp op-amp survey. That one reviewer calls the AD845 smooth, with less detail than the AD843 and a slightly valve-like feel while keeping ADI's punch. It sounds looser, softer and 'slower' than Burr-Brown parts. The reviewer ranks its resolution above OPA132/134 and AD823 and below AD843/OPA627, and recommends it for mains-powered amps. A claimed 'cult following' for DAC I/V stages remains unsourced.

families.counterfeit_notes: No AD845-specific counterfeit reports were found. General checks: (1) ADI logo, full part number with grade letter, and a plausible date code. (2) The SOIC version is a 16-lead wide body (JR-16/JRZ-16), so an 'AD845' marked on an SOIC-8 body is suspect (inferred). (3) Supply current should be about 10 mA (reviewer figure); a relabelled low-power JFET part such as a TL071 draws far less (inferred). (4) Check for slew near 100 V/us and unity-gain bandwidth of at least 12.8 MHz (datasheet). (5) Non-Z JN/KN parts reportedly went out of production around 2010, so they should carry older date codes.

families.name: AD847 / AD827 (single / dual high-speed bipolar video op amp)
families.tagline: ADI's 50 MHz, 300 V/us video op amp. In the 1990s it became a favourite CD-player and DAC upgrade, praised for fast, dynamic sound with strong bass.
families.technology: A bipolar, voltage-feedback, high-speed op amp (50 MHz unity-gain bandwidth, 300 V/us). It is internally compensated to be stable at unity gain and is rated to drive unlimited capacitive load. ADI's SPICE macro-model uses an NPN differential input pair. According to ADI's electronics textbook, the AD848 (stable at G>=5) and AD849 (stable at G>=25) are basically the same design with different internal compensation. ADI's AD827 data sheet calls it the dual version of the 'industry-standard AD847'. The fab process name (complementary bipolar or otherwise) was not verified this run.

reputation.summary: A niche-cult op amp for 1990s-era swaps. The AD847/AD827 were ADI video amplifiers that audiophiles fitted into CD-player output stages, DAC I/V and filter stages and headphone amps. The rec.audio FAQ listed the AD847/AD827 among 'the better op amps for audio'. Chinese reviewers (Soomal) group the AD847 with the AD797 as famous for big dynamics, a 'grand' sound and powerful bass. Western and Japanese listeners describe the AD827 as warm and slightly sweet, with a sharp attack, forward vocals and clean highs; some find it a little coarse or thin in the bass. It is still named as a rolling option: Fosi Audio lists the AD827 as compatible with the ZA3. All of these are subjective, anecdotal listening reports. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were found.
sonic_descriptors: a bit too sweet (AD827, Audio Asylum)
huge dynamics / grand sound (Soomal: 动态大，声音大气)
ADI 'both ends lifted' tonal tilt (两头翘, Soomal)
vocals forward, clean highs, slightly coarse (Japanese reviews)
fast, clean square-wave response without overshoot
typical_uses: CD-player analog output stage upgrades
DAC I/V conversion and output filter stages
headphone amplifiers and preamps
op-amp rolling in consumer gear (e.g. Fosi ZA3)
original design use: video and line drivers, flash-ADC input buffers, cable driving (unlimited capacitive load)
caveats: Bipolar input with microamp-level bias current (about 3 uA per the ATE-25 table): DC offset rises with high-impedance or unmatched source resistances. Check DC-coupled stages. The AD827's offset is specified at 2 mV max.
A 50 MHz part in sockets or adapters needs tight supply decoupling and short leads. This is general high-speed practice, not a documented AD827-specific failure.
It is specified from +/-5 V to +/-15 V and draws about 5 mA per amp, more than audio parts such as the NE5532-class alternatives.
The AD827 surface-mount version is a 16-lead SO (R-16: AD827JR-16 / AD827JRZ-16), so only the DIP-8 version is a drop-in for standard dual sockets. The non-Z AD827JR-16 is obsolete at Digi-Key.
Some listeners find it too sweet, or light and loose in the bass. One Japanese headphone-amp test reported reduced gain below about 200 Hz and a 'sparse' impression (anecdotal).

families.counterfeit_notes: No AD847- or AD827-specific counterfeit reports were found. Marketplace listings such as '2pieces AD827 AD827JN AD827JNZ DIP-8 Fever Dual Op Amp' on Amazon, eBay and AliExpress come from unknown sellers, and older non-Z 'JN' stock is a typical remarking target. Buy from ADI or authorised distributors (Digi-Key, Mouser, Arrow still listed AD827JNZ in 2026). The AD827 data sheet ordering guide confirms that the only surface-mount AD827 is a 16-lead plastic SO (R-16: AD827JR-16, now obsolete at Digi-Key, and AD827JRZ-16). Any 'AD827' in SOIC-8 is therefore not a genuine ADI package and should be treated as a remark. Discrete modules marketed as 'replace AD827' are not AD827s. Beyond the package fact, this advice is inferred (low confidence).

reputation.summary: This is a niche, engineer-oriented part rather than an op-amp-rolling favourite. ADI markets it for high-fidelity audio and instrumentation where power is limited. ADI app note AN-1429 recommends it for the I/V stage of current-output audio DACs. The Matrix Audio Mini-i Pro 2S uses it for the DAC low-pass filter and to drive a TPA6120A2 headphone stage (LME49720 does the I/V). Soomal groups it with the LME49720 as a 'very high-end low-distortion op amp'. The claim that it is a drop-in NE5532 upgrade comes only from the discovery note and was not verified. No ASR, Head-Fi or diyAudio listening or measurement reports were retrieved.
sonic_descriptors: low distortion (Soomal: 'very high-end low-distortion op amp'; ADI 0.0002% THD+N typ)
low noise at low supply current (vendor positioning)
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) conversion
DAC post-filter / low-pass stage
headphone amplifier input or pre-driver stage (e.g. ahead of a TPA6120A2)
low-power, small-enclosure or high-density audio
NE5532 replacement where supply current is limited (discovery note, unverified)
caveats: The minimum specified supply is 9 V total, so it is unsuitable for a single 5 V or +/-2.5 V rail (AN-1429).
Output is not rail-to-rail. About 2 V of headroom to each rail limits swing on low supplies (AN-1429).
Bipolar input means current noise matters. A Japanese measurement-ADC designer chose the FET-input OPA1656 instead because of kilohm-level resistor networks.
It is SMD-only (SOIC-8 or 2x2 mm LFCSP), so socket rolling needs a DIP adapter.
Confirm the datasheet maximum supply before putting it in an NE5532 socket at +/-18 V or above.

reputation.summary: A niche part in DIY DAC circles. On diyAudio it comes up as a current-to-voltage (I/V) choice after current-output DACs, including in 'best dual I/V op amp these days' threads. Builders cite its very low voltage noise, bandwidth and ±16 V headroom. ADI pitches it for 16-bit and 18-bit systems. It is also used in instrumentation LNAs and photodetectors, such as Gerhard Hoffmann's 'lono' parallel-op-amp LNA. One audio review site calls the ADA4898-1 a cheap 0.9 nV/√Hz equivalent of the LT1115. The praise quotes come from the discovery notes and were not re-checked by web search.
sonic_descriptors: deep, tight and impactful bass (diyAudio, I/V use; per discovery notes, not re-checked)
excellent in DAC I/V stages (diyAudio; per discovery notes)
typical_uses: I/V converter after current-output audio DACs
DAC output buffer / reconstruction filter
Low-noise preamp / LNA front ends (parallel arrays, as in Hoffmann 'lono' and aewallin ADA4898_LNA)
Photodiode transimpedance and servo loops
16-bit/18-bit ADC drivers (ADI's stated target)
caveats: Comes only in SOIC-8 with an exposed pad. There is no DIP version, so op-amp rolling needs an adapter. The pad may be tied to −VS or left floating, but never to ground or +VS.
Draws about 7.9 mA per amplifier, so a dual dissipates about 0.47 W at ±15 V. It runs warm on DIP adapters that have no copper under the pad.
Needs at least ±5 V, so it does not suit low-voltage portable designs.
Current noise is fairly high (2.4 pA/√Hz). The noise-optimal source impedance is about 375 Ω, so it works best with low-impedance sources.
General high-speed caution (engineering inference): with 50 to 65 MHz of bandwidth, layout, decoupling and capacitive loading matter. Socket or adapter wiring can cause peaking or oscillation.

families.name: HA-2600 / HA-2602 / HA-2605 and HA-2620 / HA-2622 / HA-2625 (Harris high-input-impedance bipolar singles)
families.tagline: Harris 500 Mohm bipolar singles: HA-2600/2605 (12 MHz, 7 V/us) and uncompensated HA-2620/2625 (100 MHz GBW, 35 V/us, gain >5). Jung-era audio praise unverified.
families.technology: Bipolar single op-amps with very high input impedance (500 Mohm, HA-2600/HA-2620) per Intersil/Renesas datasheets. HA-2600/2602/2605 are internally compensated (12 MHz unity-gain bandwidth, 7 V/us, 150 kV/V). HA-2620/2622/2625 are the 'very wideband, uncompensated' versions (100 MHz GBW, stable for closed-loop gain >5, 35 V/us, 150 kV/V). Dielectric-isolation process and input-stage topology were not confirmed from a datasheet this run.

reputation.summary: No Hi-Fi community praise was verified. No search budget was spent on reputation this run. Discovery notes say these Harris parts were cited in late-1970s/1980s Walt Jung-era audio literature as high-slew, high-impedance options, and that modern enthusiast praise is minimal. Treat this as a historical tier-C entry until the Jung citations are confirmed.
typical_uses: High-slew line-level and instrumentation stages in the slew-induced-distortion era (per discovery notes, unverified)
High-gain amplification of fast wideband signals from high-impedance sources (HA-2620/2625 at gain >5, per the datasheet description)
caveats: HA-2620/2622/2625 are uncompensated and stable only at closed-loop gains greater than 5 (datasheet). Do not use them as unity-gain followers or in low-gain audio stages.
HA3-2625-5 is obsolete per distributors. Other codes probably come only from surplus, new-old stock or Rochester Electronics.
Grade-specific values here come from EWB/MicroSim simulator libraries. Only headline typicals were confirmed from datasheets.
Noise (e_n, i_n), THD, quiescent current and supply range were not verified.

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit or remarking reports were found. This run used no search on it, so this is a gap, not a clean bill. HA3-2625-5 is obsolete per distributors. Current supply is likely surplus, new-old stock or Rochester Electronics, which has a datasheet copy filed under HA2-2625-5 on Octopart. For surplus parts, check that logos and date codes match the Harris or Intersil era. Measure the slew rate (about 7 vs about 35 V/us) and unity-gain stability to tell a 2600-series die from an uncompensated 2620-series die: a 2620/2625 will oscillate as a follower.

families.name: LF355 / LF356 / LF357 (LF155 series)
families.tagline: National's 1975 BI-FET original: the first monolithic JFET-input op amp, with 12 nV/√Hz, 12 V/µs and fast settling. A Jung-era classic that TI still makes as the LF356.
families.technology: National BI-FET: an ion-implanted p-channel JFET input pair with JFET current-source loads, plus bipolar gain and output stages on one die. It is an internally compensated single; the LF357 is decompensated and needs AV≥5. Offset null is on pins 1/5, with the 25 k pot wiper to V+. LF155/LF255/LF355 is the low-current 2.5 MHz version, LF156/LF256/LF356 the 5 MHz version, and LF157/LF257/LF357 the 20 MHz version. TI qualified BI-FET production at its FFAB wafer fab in 2018 (PCN 20180920003.1).
manufacturers: Precision Monolithics Inc. (PMI, second source c.1978)
SGS-Thomson / STMicroelectronics (second source LF355/LF356/LF357, own datasheet 'Wide bandwidth single J-FET operational amplifiers')

lineage.notes: The 1975 'New Products' page introduces the LF156 as 'the first monolithic JFET input operational amplifier' (TI still uses this wording on its LF356-MIL page). The 1980 Linear Databook covers LF155/6/7 with A and B grades. Datasheet DS005646 has May 2000 and Dec 2001 editions. Electronics (8 Jun 1978) says the LF356 fell from 'its initial $2 plus' to 75 cents.

lineage.role: second source; also made the improved OP-15/16/17
lineage.notes: Electronics, 8 Jun 1978: 'besides second-sourcing a better-performing LF356, PMI is making … OP-15, -16, and -17'. Jung (Electronic Design, 1978) says OP15/16/17 are 'patterned after the 355/356/357'. Not web-confirmed this run.
LT macromodels exist for LF155/LF155A/LF156/LF156A/LF355/LF355A/LF356/LF356A, each tagged 'JFET Input, Low IOS 10pA max'. No LF157/LF357 model was found.
The Motorola PSpice library (MOTOR.LIB) contains an LF356 model, 'LF356M'.

ST published its own LF355/LF356/LF357 datasheet titled 'Wide bandwidth single J-FET operational amplifiers' (copies on alldatasheet.com #22739 and datasheetspdf.com). The SGS PSpice library has LF355S, LF356S and LF357S. Tangent's notes (2005 Chinese translation) say ST and Fairchild still made the family after National stopped.
The only evidence is Tangent's remark in the Chinese translation. Low confidence.

TI reissued the datasheet as SNOSBH0 (Rev B and C in Mar 2013, Rev D in Nov 2015; Rev D still current Sep 2026). Product folders are LF156, LF256, LF356 and a separate LF356-MIL (Active); no '-N' rename. PCN 20180920003.1 (approved 19-Sep-2018) qualified TI's BI-FET technology at wafer fab 'FFAB' and lists LF356 wafer, H, M and N devices.

key_specs.value: ±13 V typ (±12 min) into 10 kΩ; ±12 V typ (±10 min) into 2 kΩ. Short circuit is continuous. No numeric output-current spec, only typical current-limit curves. Stable with capacitive loads up to 0.01 µF (the feature list says 10,000 pF in 1980 and 5,000 pF from 2000).

IB 30 pA typ; max 200 pA (LF35x), 100 pA (LF15x/25x/356B), 50 pA (1980 A grades). IOS 3 pA typ; max 50 pA (LF35x) or 20 pA. LT's second-source models claim 10 pA max IOS. IB roughly doubles every 10 °C of junction temperature.

key_specs.value: 3 mV typ; 10 mV max (LF35x), 5 mV max (LF15x/25x/356B). 1980 A grades: 1 mV typ / 2 max. Drift 5 µV/°C typ (A grade 3 typ / 5 max). Trimming adds only about 0.5 µV/°C per mV of adjustment.
Ion-implanted p-channel JFET differential pair with JFET current-source loads, followed by a bipolar stage (BI-FET)
key_specs.source: Electronics 8 Jun 1978 (Russell & Frederiksen, National); LT macromodel 'PFET INPUT'; TI LF356-MIL description (BI-FET technology)

key_specs.value: CMRR and PSRR 100 dB typ (min 80 for LF35x, 85 for others). AVOL 200 V/mV typ. CM range +15.1 V / −12 V typ (LF35x guaranteed only +10/−10 V).

reputation.summary: Historically important more than currently praised. The LF156/LF356 was National's first BI-FET op amp (1975) and, in National's and TI's own words, the first monolithic JFET-input op amp. Walt Jung's 1978 Electronic Design survey groups the 355/356/357 as 'second-generation FET' op amps with better drift and offset than general-purpose parts, and notes the OP-15/16/17 were 'patterned after' them. National's 1978 Electronics article stresses its low noise (12 nV/√Hz), fast settling and capacitive-load stability. Current Hi-Fi/DIY praise is thin: Tangent's headphone op-amp notes (2005 Chinese translation) liken the LF355 to the TL071 and find it unsuitable for low-impedance headphones. It survives in vintage synth, sample-and-hold, I/V and lab front-end circuits. No modern distortion measurements (ASR, Groner) were found; forum reputation was not re-searched this run.
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage converters and fast D/A or A/D buffers (fast settling)
High-impedance buffers, photodiode and electrometer front ends
Integrators, sample-and-hold, log amplifiers
Active filters and vintage analog synth VCO/VCF circuits
1970s–80s 'Jung-era' audio/line stages as a low-noise FET single
caveats: If an input goes past the negative common-mode limit (−12 V typ, only −10 V guaranteed for LF35x at ±15 V) the output is forced high, so the phase reverses. An input taken below V− can destroy the part (datasheet Application Hints).
Fitting it backwards in a socket, or reversing the supply, can fuse internal conductors (datasheet warning). This matters when op-amp rolling.
Supply current is high for a FET single: 5 mA typ, 10 mA max for the LF356. Self-heating raises input bias current, which doubles every 10 °C.
The LF357/LF157/LF257 is decompensated and stable only at AV≥5. It will oscillate as a follower or unity-gain stage, so it is not a drop-in for an LF356 socket.
Offset trim uses a 25 kΩ pot with the wiper to V+, not V−; pins 1 and 5 are BALANCE.
Poor at driving low impedances: Tangent found it unsuitable for low-impedance headphones.
It is a single (DIP-8 single pinout), so rolling it into dual-op-amp sockets needs adapters.
The earliest LF156 (1975 New Products page) labelled pin 8 'current source reference' and required pin 8 to be tied to pin 7 when offset adjust was unused. Later datasheets show pin 8 as NC.
Specs are guaranteed at ±15 V for LF35x. There is no low-voltage specification.
Post-2018 TI parts may come from a different wafer fab (PCN 20180920003.1, FFAB BI-FET qualification); datasheet limits are unchanged.

families.counterfeit_notes: No documented counterfeit reports found; forums were not searched in this run. Generic screening heuristics, not reported cases: remarked LF351/TL081-class parts are the obvious risk. A genuine LF356 draws about 5 mA typ (10 max) at ±15 V; an LF351 about 1.8 mA. Genuine GBW is about 5 MHz, and offset nulls with a 25 kΩ pot on pins 1/5 with the wiper to V+. Current TI marking is 'LF 356N' (PDIP) or 'LF356 M' (SOIC) per the SNOSBH0D addendum. Treat marketplace 'NS LF357H' metal cans and 'National' parts with post-2012 date codes as suspect. A metal-can LF357 stable as a unity-gain follower is also suspect (the real part needs AV≥5).
alternatives: TI LF356M/MX/N /NOPB or LF356-MIL: the same family, still in production
ADI (PMI) OP-15/OP-16/OP-17: improved successors 'patterned after the 355/356/357'; obsolete but found as NOS
TI OPA1641 / OPA827: modern low-noise JFET-input audio singles
ADI AD8610 / ADA4627-1: fast-settling precision JFET singles
ADI (LT) LT1122: fast-settling JFET single for I/V and sample-and-hold duty
TI TL071H: cheap modern JFET single with similar speed (Tangent likens the LF355 to the TL071)
TI OPA140 / OPA1655: modern low-noise precision singles

reputation.summary: A fast 1970s bipolar op-amp (15 MHz, 50 V/us min). It is reportedly among the high-slew parts favoured in the late-1970s slew-induced-distortion/TIM debate (Walter Jung et al., Audio magazine), but the specific articles were not verified. Today it is a niche part in DIY circles for fast buffers and DAC I/V stages. Community evidence is thin: there are no published noise specs and no measured reviews were found. It is not a low-noise audio design. Some hobby write-ups wrongly call it a dedicated audio op-amp.
typical_uses: DAC output buffer / I-V stage (DIY)
fast line buffers
active video filters and video receivers
function generators / oscillators
fast D/A output amplifiers, pulse amplifiers
class-D amplifier control loop (academic paper)
caveats: High-speed part: bypass pins 4 and 7 with 0.1 uF capacitors placed right at the pins. It is prone to oscillation with stray capacitance on the inverting input and with long socket/adaptor leads.
Pins 1/5/8 are compensation/balance pins, so feed-forward-compensated circuits are not drop-in with parts that use pin 8 as NC or pins 1/5 as offset null.
Feed-forward compensation (>150 V/us) applies only to inverting configurations.
Quiescent current is about 5 mA typ per amp (third-party figure).
Needs at least ±5 V supplies.
No noise specification. Not a low-noise part compared with NE5534/LME49710-class devices.
TI sells two separate LM318 lines (LM318 / SLOS063 and LM318-N / SNOSBS8), and LTC made its own version, so behaviour may differ by maker.

families.counterfeit_notes: No specific LM318 counterfeit reports were found. General precaution for cheap marketplace DIP-8 LM318N parts: they may be remarked slower op-amps. As a quick check, run a unity-gain square wave at ±15 V. A genuine part slews at least 50 V/us, while a remarked 741/4558-class part slews under about 1-2 V/us. This is generic advice, not a documented LM318 case. Note also that LM318M (National SOIC) is reported obsolete, so new-stock offers of it deserve extra scrutiny.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part. In the diyAudio thread 'The best sounding audio integrated opamps', one experienced listener names the LME49723 among the 'absolute best sounding' VFB op-amps (with LT1028, OPA132UA, LME49720HA) and his favourite plastic-DIP op-amp, reporting fuller bass and more detail than the LM4562/LME49720 but sometimes too much clarity and thin body on high violin notes. A Head-Fi comment (attribution unconfirmed) says it differs from the LM4562/LME49720/LME49860 more than they differ from each other. AudioKarma members included it in CD-player op-amp rolls where the OPA2604 and a Sparkos discrete were preferred. No objective measurement review was found.
sonic_descriptors: fuller, more convincing bass dynamics and body (one listener)
more detail than the LM4562/LME49720 (one listener)
on some recordings too much clarity, thin body on high violin notes (one listener)
sounds more different from the LM4562/LME49720/LME49860 than they do from each other (unconfirmed attribution)
typical_uses: DIP-8 op-amp rolling in CD players, DACs and preamps
Op-amp upgrades in headphone amps and line stages
SOIC-8 audio stages in DIY designs, e.g. Rezzonics NuTube overdrive and NuTubeAmp (LME49723MA/NOPB in BOMs)
caveats: TI lists the device as NRND.
The DIP version is reportedly scarce and was not found at distributors in 2026 searches; most supply is SOIC-8, needing an adapter for socket rolling.
Praise comes from a handful of listeners; no published measurements found.
AudioKarma advises careful decoupling against oscillation for the sister LME49720; no LME49723-specific report found.
Split-supply part (±2.5 V minimum), not a low-voltage single-supply op-amp; one hobby project replaced it with an MCP6001 for that reason.

families.tagline: National's late Overture E-Series JFET dual (7 nV/√Hz, 0.00003% THD+N). It came only in PSOP, is now obsolete, and Japanese op-amp rollers run it on DIP adapters.
families.technology: Dual JFET-input audio op-amp from National's LME 'Overture E-Series' (siblings: LME49720, LME49860, LME49990). The datasheet says the JFET process was used to lower flicker noise and the noise corner frequency. Supply range is ±5 V to ±17 V. It is unity-gain stable, drives capacitive loads up to 100 pF, and has typical input bias of 5 pA. The only package is an 8-lead PSOP with an exposed pad (MR suffix; TI's package addendum calls it 'SO PowerPAD').

part_numbers.notes: Generic dual. No single, quad or vendor DIP version has been seen. TI discontinued it as part of a process-technology end-of-life and names OPA1642 as the replacement (TI E2E thread 565578, about 2016-2017).

families.counterfeit_notes: No LME49880-specific counterfeit reports were found. TI has obsoleted the part (process-technology end-of-life, about 2016-2017), so any 'new' stock is old inventory, broker stock or pre-mounted DIP adapter boards. reputation.summary: Linear Technology's dedicated ultralow-noise audio op amp. Its datasheet called it 'the lowest noise audio operational amplifier available', which is a vendor claim from 1989. Enthusiasts have long used it in low-source-impedance stages: MC/MM phono (RIAA) preamps, MC head amps and microphone preamps. The 1990s rec.audio FAQ said the LT1028 and LT1115 'are very well received for phono preamps, head amplifiers, and microphone preamplifiers'. diyAudio members call it 'very interesting sounding' and group it with the LT1028 and LT1122. Japanese hobbyists call it the most monitor-like LT part and use it in phono-EQ builds. A srad.jp commenter said its datasheet noise equals the AD797's at about half the Mouser price. Audiokarma has a thread on LT1115 op amps. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurement was located.
sonic_descriptors: clean and quiet with low-impedance sources
typical_uses: MC/MM phono RIAA equaliser / preamp
moving-coil head amp
microphone preamplifier
low-noise instrumentation / measurement preamp with low source impedance
single-op-amp socket rolling in DIY gear
caveats: Single only (no dual or quad), so dual sockets need an adapter.
The only SMD version is the 16-lead wide SOIC (SW16), which has a non-standard single pinout. No SO-8 exists, and the tin-lead LT1115CSW is obsolete at Mouser.
Expensive: about 20 USD according to Frieve, against about 2.7 USD for the ADA4898-1 with similar noise.
The noise is optimised for low source impedance. With high-impedance sources, current noise (about 1.2 pA/rtHz) cancels the benefit.

The rec.audio FAQ claimed it is 'not unity gain stable', but the LTC macromodel says it is internally compensated. The minimum stable gain was not confirmed this run. With 40 MHz+ GBW, careful layout and decoupling are needed.

families.technology: Single-channel, voltage-feedback, internally compensated (unity-gain stable) op-amp with JFET inputs. reputation.summary: A niche, cult-level pick with no mainstream following. Head-Fi op-amp rollers name the LT1122 as a candidate alongside the LT1361, LT1364 and LT1469 in a thread on DAC output stages. diyAudio members group it with the LT1028 and LT1115 as Linear Technology chips worth trying and call the LT1122ACN8 'a good chip' (second-hand, unverified wording). Tangent's op-amp listening notes (Chinese translation on Soomal, 2005) list it among chips to test later, with no verdict. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements are known. Outside audio, a KiCad reproduction of the HP 3458A A3 board uses an LT1122 as unity-gain buffer U404.
sonic_descriptors: 'a good chip' (diyAudio, general praise; no specific sonic descriptors verified)
typical_uses: DAC output and reconstruction-filter stages (Head-Fi recommendations)
Single op-amp rolling in DIP-8 sockets (LT1122ACN8 / CCN8)
Fast-settling buffers for 12-bit data conversion and acquisition (datasheet design intent)
Precision instrument buffers: HP 3458A A3 board U404 (KiCad reproduction)
caveats: Single channel only: dual-op-amp sockets need an adapter carrying two of them.
About 7 mA quiescent current per amplifier (datasheet), so it runs warmer and drains batteries faster than TL07x-class parts.
Fast part (14 MHz, 80 V/us): treat like other fast op-amps (good decoupling, short leads); stability in a given socket not verified.
Grades A-D probably differ in DC or settling guarantees (not verified); for audio the grade is unlikely to matter.
Voltage-noise density and THD were not confirmed; the datasheet markets speed and settling, not low noise, so do not assume it is a low-noise audio part.

families.name: LT1357 / LT1358 / LT1359 (single/dual/quad 25 MHz, 600 V/µs C-Load bipolar)
families.tagline: Lower-power (2 mA/amp) sibling of the LT1364, rated 25 MHz and 600 V/µs. A niche sound-card buffer pick that forum listeners call warm, bright and tonally rich.
families.technology: Bipolar, built on Linear Technology's complementary bipolar process. It is a single-stage voltage-feedback amplifier with matched high-impedance inputs and the slewing performance of a current-feedback amplifier, and it is stable with any capacitive load (C-Load). Per the ADI/Linear datasheets, the single-stage design settles well. The family comes in 25, 50 and 70 MHz versions at about 2, 4 and 6 mA per amplifier, each as a single, dual and quad. The LT1357 datasheet's front-page typical application is a DAC I-to-V converter.
manufacturers: Analog Devices (acquired Linear Technology in 2017; current vendor)

reputation.summary: A niche pick from the op-amp-rolling era of sound cards (Asus Xonar, Audiotrak Prodigy HD2). Forum posts describe the LT1358 as 'warm, bright, tonal rich and sounds forward'. Some posters prefer it to the faster, higher-current LT1364 in buffer duty, and it is named alongside the LT1364 and LT1361 for buffer positions. The evidence is subjective forum impressions only. No Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or other measurement data was found for the LT1357/8/9.
typical_uses: Sound-card op-amp swaps (Asus Xonar, Audiotrak Prodigy HD2 buffer/output stage)
Buffer and I/V stages in DIY DACs (the LT1357 datasheet's front-page application is a DAC I-to-V converter)
Wideband amplifiers, buffers, active filters, data acquisition and video/cable drivers (datasheet application list)
caveats: The praise rests on a few subjective forum posts from one discovery lens, and those posts were not re-checked in this pass, so confidence is low.
This is a 25 MHz / 600 V/µs part: keep the layout tight and decouple locally. C-Load stability helps with capacitive loads but not with poor bypassing or long socket leads.

This is a low-power (2.5 mA max per amplifier) part. The datasheet guarantees ±12.5 V into 500 Ω, but output current was not verified, so check it before driving headphones or low impedances directly.
Bipolar inputs: input bias current is up to 500 nA max. Watch for offset with high source impedances.
The supply range is ±2.5 V to ±15 V, so ±15 V is the top of the range and a ±18 V rail is out of spec.

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit or remark reports specific to the LT1357/LT1358/LT1359 were found. Web search this pass was limited to five queries, so this is not a clean bill of health. Buy from authorized ADI distributors, and treat marketplace 'LT1358' DIP-8s with suspicion, especially leaded (non-#PBF) parts sold as new. A bench check helps: a slow part remarked as an LT1358 cannot reach about 600 V/µs slew or 25 MHz GBW, and supply current should be at most 2.5 mA per amplifier. Also compare the laser marking and date code against known-genuine Linear/ADI parts.

families.name: LT1360 / LT1361 / LT1362 (50MHz, 800V/us C-Load bipolar single/dual/quad)
families.tagline: Linear Tech's 50MHz/800V/us C-Load bipolar op amp. Sound-card op-amp swappers rate it for DAC I/V stages and describe it as 'extremely clear and airy'.
families.technology: A voltage-feedback op amp built on Linear Technology's complementary bipolar process. It is unity-gain stable and belongs to LTC's C-Load high-speed family (LT1354 to LT1365). The C-Load design keeps it stable with any capacitive load: it senses the pole the load puts on the output and adds compensation at the gain node. The input stage is matched and high-impedance and the part slews like a current-feedback amplifier; that part of the description comes from the family text in the LT1364/LT1365 datasheet.

reputation.summary: A niche favourite of sound-card op-amp swappers (mostly Asus Xonar Essence ST/STX), used mainly in the I/V stage after current-output DACs. One user paired it with an LME49720 and described the result as an 'extremely clear and airy sound'. Some Xonar/Head-Fi threads list it with the LT1028, OPA627, OPA827, LT1364 and LT1469 as I/V or DAC-output choices. Users also call it forgiving of poor bypassing. All of this is subjective forum opinion from a handful of posts; no bench measurements (Audio Science Review, Samuel Groner or similar) were found.
typical_uses: I/V conversion after current-output DACs (Asus Xonar Essence ST/STX)
DAC output buffer / filter stage
sound-card op-amp swapping
wideband amplifiers, buffers, active filters, cable drivers (vendor applications)
caveats: Forum posts say the dual comes only in SOIC-8, so DIP-8 sockets need an adapter. A DIP-8 LT1361CN8#PBF appears only in a part sitemap and is unconfirmed.
Bipolar inputs with fairly high bias current (LCSC parametric: 300 nA) and up to 1 mV offset: expect DC offset with high source or feedback impedances.
A 50MHz, 800V/us part: needs a tight layout and short decoupling. Socket adapters add parasitics, although the C-Load design is stable with capacitive loads.
Up to 5 mA per amplifier. The 34 mA output-current figure (distributor data) suggests it should not drive low-impedance headphones directly.
Descriptors come from a small number of subjective posts; no measurements were found.

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit or remarking reports specific to the LT1360/LT1361/LT1362 were found. Genuine LT1361CS8 parts come in several marking styles: an ink top mark on older parts, a laser top mark after ADI PCN 21_0060, and, after PCN 24_0236 (Oct 2024), the trace code on top instead of the bottom. A marking-style difference alone does not prove a fake. Buy from ADI or authorized distributors; pulled or grey-market high-speed LTC parts are common on marketplace sites. A DIP-8 'LT1361' deserves scrutiny: the DIP-8 orderable LT1361CN8#PBF appears only in a part sitemap and is unconfirmed.

reputation.summary: A niche but well-regarded MUSES model in the Japanese DIY and portable-audio community. It is the MUSES pick when a low-voltage or battery supply rules out the higher-voltage parts. A Zigsow user review ('低電圧で使えて優しい音質', 'usable at low voltage, gentle sound') finds it gentler than the OPA2134 while keeping MUSES-like transparency. A Stereo magazine blog article groups it with MUSES8820 and MUSES8920 as the mass-production MUSES models. No English-language objective measurements (ASR, Groner) were found.
sonic_descriptors: gentle / soft (優しい音質), per a Zigsow review
typical_uses: battery-powered portable headphone amplifiers
portable audio devices and smartphones (vendor-stated targets; leadless KW1 aimed at mobile)
high-end audio equipment (vendor-stated)
low-voltage single-supply (+2.7 V and up) audio stages
Audio-Technica AT-PHA100 portable DAC/amp, reportedly (only from an AI-generated review repo; low confidence)
caveats: There is no vendor DIP8 version. DIP8 'units' (for example Audiophonics) are SOP8 dies on adapter boards, and adapters add their own layout and stability risk.
It is a low-voltage part. The listed operating range tops out at about 13 V total, and the maximum is about 15 V per parametric data. Do not roll it into +/-15 V equipment.
Almost all praise comes from Japanese subjective reviews. No independent measurement data was located.

reputation.summary: Too new (October 2025) for a settled enthusiast consensus. Most of the praise is the vendor's own claim, repeated by Japanese and international trade press: MUSES flagship sound-tuning methods were applied to MUSES8920/A by reviewing the signal and power paths and optimising element placement. Japanese DIY blogger new_western_elec compared it with NL8902 (Oct 2025) and published a listening post, 'MUSES8921を試聴しました' (Apr 2026). Per a search summary of that post, he treats MUSES8920 -> 8920A -> 8921 as step-wise version upgrades of the JFET MUSES line, and hears 8920A as slightly shallower and narrower in space than 8920 but wider in bandwidth. His specific MUSES8921 verdict was not captured. No ASR, Groner or other independent measurements were found. The headline typical specs equal MUSES8920A's, so any improvement is a sound/layout claim, not a spec gain.
sonic_descriptors: Vendor marketing only: 'true sound that resonates with the heart' (心に響く"真実の音") (Macnica/Nisshinbo launch headline)
Vendor claim: better sound than MUSES8920/A through signal/power-path review and element-placement optimisation
new_western_elec (per search summary, Apr 2026): part of a step-wise 8920 -> 8920A -> 8921 evolution; detailed MUSES8921 descriptors not captured
Predecessor MUSES8920, NOT MUSES8921 (JP community folklore, not re-verified): clean and dry, high resolution, no harshness
typical_uses: DAC I/V converter (5 pA input bias; the vendor says it is ideal for this)
Preamplifier / line amplifier
Active filters
Headphone amplifiers, including portable (vendor target market)
PC, desktop and portable audio (vendor target market)
Op-amp rolling via the Kyoritsu MUSES8921AN-DIP conversion module
caveats: Different part number from MUSES8920/MUSES8920A; do not treat it as the same die.
Headline typical specs (8.0 nV/rtHz, 0.0004%, 25 V/us, 11 MHz, 5 pA, ±3.5 to ±17 V) match MUSES8920A's; measured benefits are unproven.
No independent measurements or ASR/Groner data found.
Retail 'DIP' units seen in Japan are the SMD MUSES8921AN on an adapter board (Kyoritsu MUSES8921AN-DIP), not a native DIP8, so check the height and fit in sockets.
Costs more at retail than MUSES8920AE (about ¥1,700 vs ¥1,200 in Japanese listings; the MUSES8921 price probably includes the adapter).

Long-term supply of the MUSES line is uncertain. new_western_elec reported (2024-06 factory visit) that MUSES05 and MUSES03 were dropped, and he voiced concern after Nisshinbo HD news in Dec 2025 (earlier pass, not re-verified).

families.counterfeit_notes: No counterfeit reports specific to MUSES8921 were found; the part has only been on sale since October 2025. General Japanese community advice (earlier pass, not re-verified) is that MUSES01/02 fakes are common on Chinese marketplaces; genuine parts are laser-marked and fakes are often ink-printed. Buy from authorised channels such as Akizuki, Kyoritsu Eleshop/Digit, Mouser and DigiKey. Be sceptical of any bare 'MUSES8921D' or native-DIP8 MUSES8921: only the EMP8 MUSES8921AN is confirmed, and retail DIP units seen are Kyoritsu adapter modules (MUSES8921AN-DIP). Relabelled MUSES8920/8920A or generic JFET duals are a plausible but unverified risk. There is no same-number silicon change: MUSES8921 is a separate part number and a vendor-described derivative of MUSES8920/A.

It is the entry-level model that inherits MUSES technology and 'applies MUSES technology to a more productive technology' (https://www.nisshinbo-microdevices.co.jp/en/products/operational-amplifier/spec/?product=nl8802; https://www.mouser.com/new/nisshinbo/nisshinbo-nl8802-dual-op-amp/).

The new_western_elec blog post 'MUSES8820とNL8802、MUSES8920とNL8902を聴く' exists and compares NL8802 with MUSES8820 (https://nw-electric.way-nifty.com/blog/2025/09/post-02dac7.html).

reputation.summary: A new part with little coverage outside Japan. Most of the praise comes from new_western_elec (nw-electric.way-nifty.com), a Japanese DIY-audio blogger. In a Sept 2025 A/B session he ranked OPA2604 < MUSES8820 < MUSES8920 < NL8802 < NL8902, and he heard more high-frequency extension and more detail than MUSES8920. His Oct 2025 post compares NL8902 with the new MUSES8921. NS-kobo's phono-EQ listening comparison reportedly found NL8902AN better than OPA2604AP, with richer musical reproduction (known only from a search summary; the attribution is not fully certain). The distributor Macnica pitches it as entry-level with sound 'on par with higher-end models'. That is marketing. No measurements from Audio Science Review or other independent sources were found.
sonic_descriptors: more information/detail than MUSES8920 and NL8802 (new_western_elec ranking)
richer musical reproduction than OPA2604AP in a phono EQ (NS-kobo, via search summary)
typical_uses: op-amp rolling in DAC output, line and phono-EQ stages on EMP8-to-DIP8 adapters (community use)

Only press-release typical figures are known. The datasheet min/max tables and the datasheet version were not checked.
Supply risk: new_western_elec has voiced worry about Nisshinbo restructuring and past MUSES discontinuations (blog opinion, low confidence).
Do not confuse it with MUSES8920/8920A/8921. Those are separate part numbers, not revisions of NL8902.

families.name: OP249 (PMI / Analog Devices dual precision high-speed JFET)
families.tagline: PMI/ADI's fast (22 V/µs) precision JFET dual. The 1993 rec.audio FAQ rated it 'highly recommended', and Fosi still lists it as a DIP-8 rolling option.
families.technology: Dual precision high-speed op amp with a JFET input pair. ADI calls it a 'high speed, precision dual JFET op amp'. The PMI SPICE macromodel (JX = PJF) shows the pair is P-channel. Designed by Precision Monolithics (PMI) and continued by Analog Devices. Around 2010 the wafers moved to ADI's Wilmington fab (ADWIL), as described in PCN 10_0062.

reputation.summary: Evidence is thin and mostly historical. Bob Neidorff's rec.audio Audio FAQ (part 2, v1.5, last modified 1993-06-04) lists OP249 among its 'highly recommended' audio duals, alongside OPA2604, AD797, LT1115 and HA5112. The same FAQ says FET op amps suit line-level, high-source-impedance signals. Fosi Audio's ZA3 marketing lists OP249 among compatible DIP-8 duals for op-amp rolling. A synth-DIY CV/audio mixer (SOWA) chose it for 'low offset and good dynamic parameters', and Bordodynov's LTspice collection files it under 'AudioOpamp/AD'. No measurement-based audio reviews and no community sound descriptors were found.
typical_uses: Line-level audio stages and buffers (the FET-input use case in the 1993 rec.audio FAQ)
Op-amp rolling in DIP-8 sockets (for example the Fosi Audio ZA3)
DC-coupled CV/audio mixers in synth DIY (SOWA mixer)
caveats: The rec.audio FAQ warns that a faster op amp swapped into existing gear may oscillate, depending on design and layout. This is a general warning, not specific to OP249.

Supply current is about 5.6 mA typ (OP249G) and voltage noise is 17 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz, noisier than bipolar audio duals. Output-drive capability was not verified, so check the ADI data sheet before using it for headphone drive or low-noise duty.
Reputation rests on a 1990s FAQ and vendor marketing lists. There is no modern measured evidence of audio superiority.
Parts made before and after the fab transfer and mask change in PCN 10_0062 (about 2010) may differ slightly in offset behaviour.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OP249-specific counterfeit or remarking reports were found; this was not searched in depth. OP249 is a legacy PMI/ADI precision part that appears on broker and marketplace sites (for example Worldway Electronics and IC-listing sites). Leaded (non-Z) GP/GS parts and old ceramic parts are mostly broker stock. Compare the logo, top marking and date-code format with genuine ADI parts, and measure supply current (about 5.6 mA typ), offset and slew rate (22 V/µs typ) against the ADI data sheet. Be suspicious of any 'OP249' in unusual packages or at very low prices. Genuine parts made before and after about 2010 can differ in die and passivation (PCN 10_0062).

reputation.summary: An OEM and engineering favourite rather than an op-amp-rolling legend. It comes only in SMD packages, so enthusiasts rarely swap it. It pairs low noise and distortion with modest supply current (2.6 mA/ch). Per a TI E2E thread and Gearspace discussion (not re-checked this run), TI pointed LME49720 users to it after that part's EOL. Reported design wins come from mirrored reviews (Soomal, Frieve) and maker pages: the iBasso DX90 uses a pair of OPA1602 per channel as the DAC I/V stage (with OPA1611 and BUF634), and the Cayin RU3 dongle uses OPA1602 alongside SGM8262 in parallel drive. DIY projects use it as a transformerless balanced line driver, and the quad OPA1604 shows up in multichannel mixers. No op-amp-specific listening tests or ASR/Samuel Groner measurements were found.

reputation.summary: A tier-C 'workhorse' rather than a cult part. Makers treat it as the inexpensive surface-mount successor to OPA2134: FET input, rail-to-rail output, very low THD, 2 mA per channel. A TI E2E engineer says the two have very similar specs and swap in SO-8, but OPA1652 drives much less capacitance (about 230 pF vs 1 nF at G=−1) and has no PDIP. A Japanese zigsow review is titled 'OPA2134の後継 – OPA1652AID' (per an earlier search summary). Head-Fi 'Opamp thread' posters, as summarised by search, call it very good for a JFET-type part and under $2. One poster called it the best-sounding OPA16x2, with a forward, full-bodied presentation that is less detailed than LME49720. Another heard it as close to OPA1656, with the OPA1656 more neutral. A TI designer is quoted there as a fan of its noise performance for the price. Its real footprint is OEM portable audio. Soomal teardowns show it doing I/V and/or LPF in the FiiO X5K, VentureCraft SoundDroid Vantam and Cayin N5 MKII. It also appears in HiBy R6 PRO II / R6 III, HiBy R4 and Cayin BTC-2. The OPA1654 quad appears in Eurorack/synth designs. No independent bench measurements (ASR, Groner) were found. Most enthusiasts now point to the OPA1656 as the higher-performance OPA165x.
sonic_descriptors: Forward, 'spectator-like' soundstage with adequate body and thickness; detailed, but less so than LME49720 (single Head-Fi poster, per search summary)
Similar to OPA1656; OPA1656 a bit more linear (Head-Fi poster, per search summary)
Described as an improved OPA2134 successor (zigsow JP review, per earlier search summary)
typical_uses: DAC current-to-voltage (I/V) conversion in portable players (FiiO X5K, Cayin N5 MKII, VentureCraft Vantam)
Post-DAC low-pass filter and line-out stages
Headphone amp front end/driver ahead of discrete transistor output stages (HiBy R6 PRO II / R6 III)
SO-8 replacement for OPA2134 where the capacitive load is small
Unity-gain buffers with high-impedance sources (FET input, low current noise)
Mixers, effects, musical instruments, Eurorack (OPA1654 quad), guitar pedal output buffers
Op-amp rolling via SOIC-to-DIP adapter modules
caveats: SMD only (SOIC-8, VSSOP-8, WSON-8; quad in SOIC-14/TSSOP-14); no PDIP. Rolling needs a DIP adapter, and adapter/socket parasitics add capacitance.

Weak capacitive-load drive: 100 pF per the datasheet, and about 230 pF max at G=−1 per a TI E2E engineer, versus 1 nF for OPA2134. It is not a blind drop-in where the old circuit relied on OPA2134's cap-load tolerance. Use a series resistor of about 50 Ω.
Output drive is ±30 mA (ISC ±50 mA): not a stand-alone low-impedance headphone driver. OEMs add discrete or buffer stages.
Input common-mode range ends 2 V below V+, so it is not rail-to-rail input. Output swings to within 800 mV of each rail at 2 kΩ.
The sound impressions above come from individual forum posts and are subjective.
Noisier (4.5 vs 2.9 nV/√Hz) and slower (18 MHz and 10 V/µs vs 53 MHz and 24 V/µs) than the later OPA1656.

families.counterfeit_notes: No OPA1652/OPA1654-specific counterfeit reports were found. Counterfeits of sibling TI audio parts are documented: an 'OPA1612' that was a TL082 die (TI E2E, diyAudio) and suspected fake OPA1656 from AliExpress. Hobbyists mostly buy OPA1652 as DIP-adapter modules (AliExpress; Kyoritsu Q5M411 'OPA1652AID-DIP'), where the chip's origin cannot be verified. How to check: (1) TI never made a PDIP OPA1652, which a TI E2E engineer confirms, so a DIP-bodied 'OPA1652' chip is fake. (2) Genuine top marks per TI's 2026 addendum are 'OP1652' (SOIC-8 D and WSON DRG), 'OUPI' (VSSOP-8 DGK) and 'OPA1654' (SOIC-14/TSSOP-14), plus the TI logo and a lot code. (3) Iq should be about 2 mA per channel; input bias should be in the pA range (±100 pA max), and a bias current in the nA range points to a bipolar remark; GBW should be about 18 MHz. (4) Buy from authorised distributors.
alternatives: OPA1656 (dual) / OPA1655 (single): TI's next-generation OPA165x (SBOS901); 2.9 nV/√Hz @10 kHz, 53 MHz, 24 V/µs, 100 mA output. Closest upgrade on the same SOIC-8 pinout.
OPA1642 / OPA1641 / OPA1644: TI JFET-input SoundPlus parts, 5.1 nV/√Hz, THD+N 0.00005%. TI lists them with OPA2134 and OPA1652 as its FET-input audio duals.
OPA1678 / OPA1679: lower-cost TI CMOS audio dual/quad, 4.5 nV/√Hz. Discussed on modwiggler as an alternative to the OPA1654.
OPA1688: 36 V, 10 MHz, high-drive RRO audio op-amp.
OPA2134 (and OPA134/OPA4134): the legacy Burr-Brown FET audio op-amp OPA1652 often replaces; still available in DIP and better with capacitive loads (about 1 nF at G=−1).
OPA1612 / OPA1602 / OPA1662: bipolar alternatives when source impedance is low (lower e_n, higher i_n).

reputation.summary: It is not a socket-rolling legend because it is SMD-only. It is well regarded as an inexpensive, rugged all-rounder. A diyAudio member called it 'a very good all-round opamp at a reasonable price, like a 21st century version of the NE5532', with modest 8 nV/√Hz noise. Builders value its 36 V operation, rail-to-rail high-drive output and short-circuit protection, which let it drive headphones directly. One GitHub modder reports it as the final stage of the Topping NX4 DSD, and built an adapter to swap in the INA1620. Other reported uses include DIY headphone amps (HiFiVision build, diyAudio OPA1688/OPA1622 thread), DJ-mixer cue outputs, DAC reconstruction filters and retro-computer audio boards. Forum threads (TI E2E, AudioKarma, Head-Fi) suggest it as an SMD substitute for the discontinued OPA2604AP. TI's own 'next-generation OPA2134/OPA2604 replacement' FAQ is about the OPA1656. No Audio Science Review or Samuel Groner measurements were found.
typical_uses: Headphone driver / output stage (Topping NX4 DSD final stage per one modder; HiFiVision DIY headphone amp; DJ mixer cue output)
Line-level buffers, line-level converters and headphone pre-amps (synth DIY)
DAC output / reconstruction filter (FPGA sigma-delta DAC project)
SMD substitute for OPA2604 / OPA2134 in new designs
Retro-computer and sound-card audio outputs (ZX-Evolution rev D+, Mac NuBus PAS16 daughterboard)
caveats: Voltage noise (8 nV/√Hz) is modest next to OPA1656 (2.9 nV/√Hz), OPA1612 or OPA1602. It is not ideal for low-level sources such as phono or microphone inputs.
SMD only: OPA1688 in SOIC-8 or WSON-8, OPA1689 in SOIC-14 or VQFN-16. There is no DIP version, so socket rolling needs an adapter (WSON is hard to adapt).

Output power into low-impedance headphones is limited. One design note found OPA1688 current insufficient for a 250 mW / 18 Ω target (AarnimM22/HD800-wireless), and Topping NX4 owners swapped in the INA1620 for more drive.
Little independent measurement coverage, so the praise rests mostly on specs and value.

In the diyAudio thread 'OPA1656: High-Performance CMOS Audio Op Amp', posters said the OPA2156 has 'amazingly good distortion' and looks better than the OPA1656 in certain respects. families.name: THS4631 (single high-voltage, high-slew-rate, wideband JFET-input op amp)
families.tagline: A ±15 V JFET-input op amp with 210 MHz GBW and 1000 V/µs slew. It is a cult DAC I/V and buffer part in Japan, praised as airy and transparent once it is stable.
families.technology: TI's JFET-input high-speed voltage-feedback op amp; the datasheet calls the input stage JFET. Single channel, unity-gain stable: 325 MHz bandwidth at G=1, 210 MHz GBW. Runs on ±5 to ±15 V (10–30 V single supply). SMD only: SOIC-8 (D), HSOIC-8 PowerPAD (DDA; 'SOIC-PP' in Rev B) and HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN; 'MSOP-PP' in Rev B). Standard single-op-amp pinout: 2 = IN−, 3 = IN+, 4 = V−, 6 = OUT, 7 = V+; 1, 5 and 8 are NC. TI's documents disagree about the thermal pad. Rev B, and the layout text of the current Rev C, say the PowerPAD is 'electrically isolated from all pins and the active circuitry', recommend grounding it, and allow any potential from VS− to VS+. The new Pin Functions table in Rev C says the pad is 'internally connected to V−'.

reputation.summary: A niche cult part in the Japanese DIY and op-amp-rolling scene. It is mostly used for I/V after current-output DACs, and in headphone amps and buffers via DIP-8 conversion boards. One Ameblo blog title calls it 'the rumoured op-amp' (噂のオペアンプ). Shirokuma sells it pre-mounted on a dual 8-pin DIP board. Users report extended highs, air and transparency when it is not oscillating. A Zigsow review calls it a 'tsundere honours-student character' (ツンデレ優等生キャラ). TI's datasheet lists 'Current DAC output buffer' as an application. No Audio Science Review or other audio-band measurements are known to this record.
sonic_descriptors: 'tsundere honours student' (ツンデレ優等生): excellent once stable
typical_uses: I/V conversion after current-output DACs
DIP-8 op-amp rolling via conversion boards (e.g. Shirokuma dual board)
Headphone amp op-amp swap (e.g. Elekit TU-HP01, per the xgender-isao blog)
High-impedance wideband buffer / line driver
caveats: Oscillates easily in rolling and adapter use. Japanese users report needing an output Zobel network. TI's datasheet warns that large feedback resistors oscillate with the input capacitance and recommends a feedback capacitor, which matters for I/V stages.
Runs hot: 12.5 mA typ and 14.5 mA max quiescent current per channel in Rev C (11.5 typ / 13 max in Rev B), about 0.375 W idle at ±15 V. A dual adapter carries two chips.

The thermal pad connection is ambiguous. The current datasheet's layout text says the PowerPAD is electrically isolated, recommends ground and allows VS− to VS+. Rev C's pin table says the pad is internally connected to V−. Tying the pad to V− satisfies both readings.
SMD only, so socket use needs an adapter. It is a single, so it replaces a dual only on a dual-conversion board.
Noise is specified only above 10 kHz, and there is no audio-band THD+N spec.
Parts shipped after the March 2025 datasheet (Rev C) may be re-characterised silicon. The listening impressions (c. 2018–2020) predate this.

revision_history.changes: Initial release.

Related-products table changed. Input impedance changed from 10^9 || 6.5 to 10^9 || 3.9 (Ω || pF). Figure labels corrected from RL=499 Ω to RF=499 Ω. Large-signal transient figures and the EVM schematic added.
Tstg corrected to −65 °C to 150 °C. No electrical changes were listed.

New TI format, with Pin Functions and ESD tables. OPA656 related-product values updated. 0–70 °C columns deleted. 0.1 dB flatness with CF=8.2 pF changed from 38 to 6 MHz, and 20 MHz without CF added. Static output current changed to 180 mA typ, 120 mA min at 25 °C and 90 mA min over temperature. Iq max changed from 13 to 14.5 mA (25 °C) and from 14 to 15 mA (over temperature). 'Updated graphs with new silicon data'. Changes not listed: Iq typ 11.5 to 12.5 mA; the pin table says the thermal pad is connected to V−; package names changed to HSOIC/HVSSOP.

silicon_changes.when: Published in SLOS451C (March 2025). Rev B (Aug 2011) was still current in 2019, and TI's PSpice model dated 2020-11-02 still uses the Rev B Iq and Isc values. No PCN was located, and the physical change date is unknown. The Sep-2023 PDN20230907001 discontinued only the D and DGN tube SKUs; it is a SKU action, not evidence of a die change.
silicon_changes.identification: By datasheet only. SLOS451C (Rev C, March 2025) says 'Updated graphs with new silicon data' and carries new limits; SLOS451B (Aug 2011) describes the legacy part. The top marking is unchanged ('4631' on D/DDA, 'ADK' on DGN in both the 2017 and 2025 addenda), and no date-code cutoff or PCN was found. The '.A'/'.B' orderable suffixes are TI-wide and not evidence of a die change.
silicon_changes.summary: Rev C re-characterises the THS4631 on 'new silicon data'. Output current rises sharply (98 to 180 mA typ), quiescent current rises (11.5 to 12.5 mA typ; 13 to 14.5 mA max), and 0.1 dB flatness with CF=8.2 pF is re-specified from 38 to 6 MHz. The new pin table ties the PowerPAD to V−, while the layout text still says isolated. Headline specs are unchanged: 7 nV/√Hz, 210 MHz GBW, 1000 V/µs, ±500 µV Vos max, 100 pA Ib max. A die, fab or process change is an inference; TI does not state it.

silicon_changes.audio_impact: No listening or measurement comparison of old and new lots was found. Expect more idle heat, stronger static drive and a different response with feedback capacitance. The part is already oscillation-prone in I/V stages, so Zobel and CF values tuned on old parts may need re-checking. The Japanese impressions (c. 2018–2020) predate Rev C.
silicon_changes.compatibility_risk: medium: pinout, package and headline AC specs are unchanged. But higher Iq, a changed compensated-loop response and the ambiguous pad potential can upset marginal thermal or stability designs, or adapters that ground the pad. Tie the pad to V−.

families.counterfeit_notes: No THS4631-specific counterfeit reports are known; this pass did not search for them specifically. Genuine markings are '4631' on SOIC-8 (D) and HSOIC-8 PowerPAD (DDA), and 'ADK' on HVSSOP-8 PowerPAD (DGN). A DDA part must have an exposed pad underneath. The THS4631D and THS4631DGN tube SKUs have been obsolete since PDN20230907001 (Sep 2023), so 'new' stock under those part numbers from brokers is old or suspect. Hobbyists usually buy the part pre-mounted on DIP adapters (e.g. Shirokuma) or as bare DDA parts (e.g. eleshop.jp). Prefer authorized distributors. The marking cannot tell pre- and post-2025 silicon apart.

OPA828: modern ±18 V JFET-input audio/precision part (catalogued separately). A calmer, lower-power ±15 V I/V choice.
open_questions: Is Rev C's 'new silicon data' a real die, process, fab or leadframe change? Is there a PCN, and from which date code?
Is the DDA/DGN pad internally tied to V− on current parts? Rev C's pin table says yes; its layout text and Rev B say it is isolated.

Rev C is internally inconsistent: the Features list says 95 mA against 180 mA typ in the table; the history's '−40 °C to +125 °C' conflicts with the table's −40 to 85 °C; and the absolute maximum of 150 mA is below the 180 mA typical output current.
Which exact revisions do the Kyohritsu, Octopart (DGN), DigiKey media and alldatasheet copies hold? Only search-summary hints were available.
No SLOS451 (Rev *) copy was located.
When did the E4/G4 variants and the DDAR reel become obsolete, and under which PDN?
There are no Audio Science Review or other audio-band measurements, and it is unknown whether Japanese adapter vendors now ship Rev C silicon.

families.name: TLE2071 / TLE2072 / TLE2074 (TI Excalibur low-noise high-speed JFET-input)
families.tagline: A fast TI Excalibur JFET op-amp (10 MHz, 40 V/us). One Head-Fi CMoy builder tried about 20 chips and rated it the best cheap choice for 9 V headphone amps.
families.technology: BiFET with a P-channel JFET input pair (per the TI PSpice macromodels) and on-chip Vos trimming (per a datasheet feature bullet). TI datasheet SLOS181 title: 'Excalibur Low-Noise High-Speed JFET-Input Operational Amplifiers'. TI's product page describes it as 38 V, 10 MHz, 40 V/us, with the input range including V+ ('In to V+'). It comes as a single (TLE2071), dual (TLE2072) and quad (TLE2074), each also in a tighter A grade. Other variants are an automotive -Q1 family (SGLS226) and a TLE2074AM. reputation.summary: A niche budget favourite, not a legend. In a Head-Fi CMoy thread (c. 2007-2009), one user who tried about 20 op-amps rated the TLE2072 the best cheap op-amp for a 9 V CMoy, ahead of the OPA2132 and OPA2134. Other posts rate it above the OPA2132, OPA2134 and OPA2227 at low supply voltage, and say it draws less battery current. Sound descriptions (forward, lively midrange, textured bass, strong cymbals) are individual forum impressions. Forum lore says the TLE2072 has the better DC specs and the TLE2082 the better AC specs, although TI's macromodels for the two are identical. The open-hardware ohdsp ADC/DAC boards (2016) use the TLE2071/2072 and name the NE5532, OPA1652 and OPA1642 as alternatives. No ASR, Samuel Groner or other distortion measurement was found.
sonic_descriptors: treble that pulls off cymbals with conviction
typical_uses: 9 V battery CMoy headphone amplifiers (op-amp rolling)
Audio ADC input filter/driver (ohdsp ADC-PCM4202 boards)
DAC differential-to-single-ended output buffers (ohdsp BUF-DiffToSE-ADAU1966)
Low-noise JFET charge preamps on 9 V batteries (CERN DIY particle detector, TLE2072CP/ACP)
Upgrade for TL071/TL072/TL081 sockets (TI markets it as a direct upgrade to TL05x/TL07x/TL08x)
caveats: The praise rests on a handful of Head-Fi CMoy posts. The sound descriptors are forum folklore and no published measurements were found.
JFET voltage noise of about 11.6 nV/rtHz typ (17 max) is well above bipolar audio parts. This matters in low-impedance, high-gain stages.
Output current is modest (about 25 mA per LISO), so low-impedance headphones need a buffer.
The input range includes V+ but stops several volts above V-. Keep inputs away from the negative rail.
Per partinfo (unconfirmed), the offset-null pins are bonded out only on the ceramic JG package; on plastic DIP/SOIC, pins 1, 5 and 8 are NC.
At 10 MHz and 40-45 V/us it is faster than the TL07x it replaces. Decouple well and watch capacitive loads (general engineering caution).

families.tagline: A fast (40 V/us, 10 MHz, up to 38 V supply) TI JFET-input op-amp that Head-Fi CMoy builders called a lively, clean, detailed budget pick.
families.technology: BiFET. The input is a P-channel JFET differential pair: both TI PSpice macromodels (level 1 and level 2) use PJF devices J1/J2, and TI's product folders call it a 'JFET-input operational amplifier'. Part of TI's 'Excalibur' TLE20xx generation. Rev B of the datasheet said the family has more than twice the bandwidth and three times the slew rate of the TL07x/TL08x, with supply rails up to ±19 V. Made as a single (TLE2081), dual (TLE2082) and quad (TLE2084), each also in a tighter-offset A grade. Older datasheets also list Y chip (die) forms.

reputation.summary: This is a niche, budget-tier favourite rather than a legend. Head-Fi CMoy/portable-amp threads (c. 2007–2009) group it with its sister TLE2072 among good cheap op-amps for 9 V CMoys. Users there say the TLE2072 has the better DC specs and the TLE2082 the better AC specs, and describe the TLE2082 as 'lively, clean, detailed' and good for budget builds. No published distortion or noise measurement (ASR, Samuel Groner, diyAudio) was found, and none was searched for in this session.
typical_uses: 9 V battery CMoy headphone amplifiers (op-amp rolling)
Input/gain stage and driver for discrete-transistor headphone output stages, e.g. the ohdsp AmpTwo (2017): TLE2082 input stage, TLE2081 driving BCP53/BCP56
General fast JFET-input buffering and filtering, e.g. the SampleScope oscilloscope front end
Proposed as a replacement for the MC33182D in the Gameboy DSO project
caveats: The evidence base is small: a handful of Head-Fi CMoy threads, with no documented measurements.
JFET-input noise (about 11.6 nV/rtHz typ, per a model library) is well above bipolar audio op-amps such as the NE5532 (about 5 nV/rtHz). This matters in low-impedance or high-gain stages.
Output current is about 25 mA (LISO library), so low-impedance headphones need a buffer or discrete output stage.
It is fast (10 MHz, 40 V/us). As general engineering caution, not a documented report: use short decoupling and watch capacitive loads when rolling it into circuits designed for TL07x-class parts.
The praise dates from c.2007–09. If TI changed the die around the 2026 datasheet revision (unconfirmed), new-production parts may not match those reports.

reputation.summary: TI's ready-made current-feedback headphone driver was widely used in the 2009-2016 PC-audio and Chinese DAC/amp boom. Examples: the Asus Xonar Essence STX, Musiland Monitor sound cards, FiiO E9, and Sony PHA-1/PHA-2. It remains in current DAC/amps (SMSL, Sabaj, Aiyima, WiiM, FiiO, Shanling). Enthusiasts value its strong current drive, very low datasheet noise and distortion, and low cost. DIYers often use it as the output stage of an op-amp + CFA composite loop, e.g. OPA1602/OPA1612 + TPA6120A2 on diyAudio. Soomal tested 10-16 products using it and stresses that results depend heavily on the implementation. Measured results are mixed: designs with series output resistors show about 10 Ω output impedance (ASR on Sony PHA-1; Roland UA-M10), while well-executed composite designs measure very well.
sonic_descriptors: coarse or lacking finesse in a high-output-impedance implementation (Soomal, Sabaj A20d 2022)
typical_uses: Sound-card headphone outputs: Asus Xonar Essence STX/ST, Creative Sound Blaster ZxR / E5 / X7 / BlasterX G5, Musiland Monitor series
Portable amps and DAPs: Sony PHA-1 / PHA-2, OPPO HA-2, FiiO E9 and X7 AM5 module, Topping NX3, Shanling M5 Ultra
Desktop DAC/amps: SMSL SAP-9 / M20 / DO400, Sabaj A20d, Aiyima DAC-A10, WiiM Ultra, Roland UA-M10, Rupert Neve RNHP
Current buffer inside a VFA-CFA composite loop (OPA1602/OPA1612, OPA2134, NE5532)
DIY headphone amp boards (pavouk.org, Cocoacrumbs, Head-Fi and AMB threads)
caveats: TI's typical application uses series output resistors, so many products have high output impedance, e.g. about 10 Ω on Sony PHA-1 (ASR) and Roland UA-M10.
Very high drive can damage low-impedance headphones or IEMs if gain is not limited (Soomal warning on the Musiland Monitor 01 PS).
Very wide-bandwidth CFA: sensitive to layout, feedback-resistor value and capacitive loads. Composite loops need careful compensation. Gain-setting questions are common on TI E2E.
The PowerPAD must be soldered to a thermal via array.
Surface-mount only (PowerPAD SOIC-20 / VQFN-14), so it cannot be swapped in a DIP socket.
Needs rails of ±5 V to ±15 V. Portable designs need boost converters, and Soomal reports it performs better at higher supply voltage.

reputation.summary: A cult part among Japanese modders rather than a Western audiophile legend. The C-Area wiki describes it as NEC's audio op-amp developed from the 4558, like the JRC NJM4580. Comparing it with the NJM4580DD, the wiki says it has tighter bass, similar treble and possibly slightly lower resolution, and calls this a matter of taste. It appears widely in Japanese CD players, AV receivers, mini-systems and Tascam multitracks. The Tascam 424 MKI channel sound is partly credited to its UPC4570 + NJM4565 op-amps (JHS 424 Gain Stage). No independent measurements were found.
sonic_descriptors: tight / firm bass (compared with NJM4580DD, per C-Area wiki)
possibly slightly less resolution than NJM4580 (subjective)
typical_uses: CD player output and filter stages (Japanese domestic players)
AV receiver audio paths (Yamaha AV-S70, µPC4570G2)
mini-system audio (Sony HCD-GRX80, UPC4570C-1)
cassette multitrack channel preamps (Tascam Portastudio 424 MKI; Tascam 238S uses µPC4570HA)
preamps and tone-control kits (e.g. AIYIMA boards sold with UPC4570C)
op-amp rolling in Japanese DIY as an NJM4580 alternative
caveats: The DIP-8 µPC4570C is reportedly a maintenance (保守) product, and aftermarket supply goes through channels such as Rochester Electronics.
Minimum supply of about ±4 V (not re-confirmed) makes it unsuitable for low-voltage single-rail designs.
The SIP-9 (HA) and SOP-8 (G2) versions are not drop-in replacements for DIP-8 sockets.
The sound claims are Japanese-community folklore, and no independent distortion or noise measurements were found.

families.counterfeit_notes: No reports of counterfeit µPC4570 parts were found. The DIP µPC4570C is reportedly a maintenance product and is sold through surplus and hobby channels, such as Suzusho and AliExpress tone-control kits advertised with 'UPC4570C'. DigiKey Marketplace lists UPC4570C-A through Rochester Electronics, an authorized aftermarket source. Remarked vintage Japanese op-amps are a general risk from hobby channels. The LCSC/EasyEDA 'NEC4570G2' part has an unverified origin. The actual top-mark formats were not seen.
alternatives: NJM4580 (JRC / Nisshinbo): the closest functional counterpart, also described as 4558-derived
NJM2114 (JRC / Nisshinbo): low-noise bipolar dual used in similar Japanese equipment
NE5532 / LM833: pin-compatible generic low-noise bipolar duals
OPA1602 (TI): modern low-noise bipolar dual
LM4562 / LME49720 (TI): modern low-distortion bipolar dual
open_questions: What changed between R03DS0135 Rev.1.00 (2019-01-17) and Rev.2.00 (Feb.27.25)? Does the Renesas datasheet still list the C (DIP) and HA (SIP) packages, or only G2?

Was the 2019 renumbering from NEC G10528 to Renesas R03DS0135 purely editorial, or did it come with a fab or process change? No PCN was found, and no silicon change is recorded (unverified rather than proven).
The printed dates of the NEC editions G10528EJ7V0, EJ8V0 and JJ8V0, and the earlier editions 1 to 6, are unknown.
Which mirror holds which edition (Reichelt, alldatasheet 6770 and 1689631, Verical, datasheet4u, Scribd, datasheetq) was not seen.

The lifecycle status of each part number (C-A, G2-E1-A, HA) is unconfirmed, and no Renesas EOL notice for the UPC4570 was found. The maintenance-product status of the DIP comes only from Japanese retailers.
The ±4 to ±16 V recommended supply range was not re-confirmed in this pass.
GBW is specified at 100 kHz, so the OrCAD macromodel's unity-gain crossover of about 7 MHz is not necessarily inconsistent. Check whether the datasheet gives a separate unity-gain frequency.
Not captured: i_n, THD, quiescent current, output current, Vos and absolute maximum ratings.
The meaning of the -1 (Sony) suffix is unknown, and the lead-free meaning of -A is unconfirmed.
The introduction year is unknown.
The origin of the LCSC 'NEC4570G2' part is unknown.
The reputation sources (C-Area wiki and others) were not re-checked in this pass.

refuted_claims: The draft said it was unknown whether Renesas issued a new datasheet number or only re-covered NEC G10528. This is refuted: Renesas issued R03DS0135 (Rev.1.00 on 2019-01-17, Rev.2.00 on Feb.27.25).

The inferred URL https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet was not found. The real Renesas URLs are /en/document/dst/upc4570-datasheet and /en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet-g10528ej8v0ds00, so the inferred URL was removed from the archive seeds.

claims_confirmed: The current Renesas datasheet is R03DS0135EJ0200 Rev.2.00, dated Feb.27.25, 11 pages: https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-datasheet
An earlier edition, R03DS0135EJ0100 Rev.1.00, is dated 2019.1.17 (search summary): https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-datasheet
Renesas serves the NEC datasheet G10528EJ8V0DS00 behind its 'Old Company Name' cover: https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet-g10528ej8v0ds00
A 7th edition, G10528EJ7V0DS00, exists: https://www.renesas.com/en/document/dst/upc4570-data-sheet-g10528ej8v0ds00
The datasheet gives e_n = 4.5 nV/√Hz, SR = 7 V/µs, GBW = 15 MHz at 100 kHz, with internal compensation: https://datasheet4u.com/datasheet/NEC/UPC4570-368239
Packages are µPC4570C (8-pin DIP, 7.62 mm), µPC4570G2 (8-pin SOP, 5.72 mm) and µPC4570HA (9-pin): https://datasheet4u.com/datasheet/NEC/UPC4570-368239
The datasheet claims 3x lower noise and 7x higher GBW and slew rate than the 4558: https://cdn-reichelt.de/documents/datenblatt/A200/upc4570.pdf

The Renesas product page title is 'UPC4570 - High-Voltage, Bipolar Dual Operational Amplifier, Dual-Power Supply, Ultra Low-Noise, High-Speed, Wide Band for Consumer Products': https://www.renesas.com/en/products/upc4570
The Renesas UPC4570C product page and UPC4570C-A part-details page are live: https://www.renesas.com/en/products/upc4570c/part-details/upc4570c-a

The Renesas UPC4570G2 product page is live: https://www.renesas.com/sg/en/products/analog-products/amplifiers/operational-amplifiers/general-purpose-op-amps/upc4570g2-ultra-low-noise-high-speed-wide-band-dual-operational-amplifier
UPC4570G2-E1-A is an orderable name with distributor datasheets: https://www.ovaga.com/files/uploads/datasheets/9084f03e-30d2-4009-aa39-0d81903ea817.pdf
DigiKey Marketplace lists UPC4570C-A through Rochester Electronics: https://www.digikey.com/en/products/detail/rochester-electronics-llc/UPC4570C-A/12130950
